text: Processing should be lawful where it is necessary in the context of a contract or the intention to enter into a contract.
rewrite: Processing is lawful when it is required for the performance of a contract or the intention to form one.

text: This Regulation does not apply to the personal data of deceased persons. Member States may provide for rules regarding the processing of personal data of deceased persons.
rewrite: This Regulation does not cover the personal data of deceased individuals. Member States may establish regulations concerning the handling of such data.

text: Article 16(2) TFEU mandates the European Parliament and the Council to lay down the rules relating to the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and the rules relating to the free movement of personal data.
rewrite: Article 16(2) of the TFEU requires the European Parliament and the Council to establish regulations concerning the protection of individuals regarding personal data processing and the free movement of such data.

text: In order to fulfil the objectives of this Regulation, namely to protect the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons and in particular their right to the protection of personal data and to ensure the free movement
rewrite: To achieve the goals of this Regulation, which are to safeguard the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals, especially their right to personal data protection, and to guarantee the free movement

text: This Regulation does not apply to the processing of personal data by a natural person in the course of a purely personal or household activity and thus with no connection to a professional or commercial activity. Personal or
rewrite: This Regulation does not apply to the processing of personal data by a natural person for purely personal or household purposes, without any link to a professional or commercial activity. Personal or

text: The controller should use all reasonable measures to verify the identity of a data subject who requests access, in particular in the context of online services and online identifiers. A controller should not retain personal data for the sole purpose of being able to react to potential requests.
rewrite: The controller must employ all reasonable methods to confirm the identity of a data subject seeking access, especially within online services and for online identifiers. Personal data should not be kept by a controller solely to address possible future requests.

text: The possibility for the controller or processor to use standard data-protection clauses adopted by the Commission or by a supervisory authority should prevent controllers or processors neither from including the
rewrite: The option for the controller or processor to employ standard data-protection clauses approved by the Commission or a supervisory authority should not hinder controllers or processors from incorporating the

text: In order to strengthen and harmonise administrative penalties for infringements of this Regulation, each supervisory authority should have the power to impose administrative fines. This Regulation should indicate
rewrite: To enhance and standardize administrative penalties for violations of this Regulation, each supervisory authority must possess the authority to levy administrative fines. This Regulation should specify

text: The processing of personal data should also be regarded to be lawful where it is necessary to protect an interest which is essential for the life of the data subject or that of another natural person. Processing of personal data
rewrite: The handling of personal data should also be considered lawful when it is essential to safeguard a vital interest for the life of the data subject or another individual. Processing of personal data

text: Moreover, the processing of personal data by official authorities for the purpose of achieving the aims, laid down by constitutional law or by international public law, of officially recognised religious associations, is carried out on grounds of public interest.
rewrite: Furthermore, the handling of personal information by public bodies to fulfill objectives established by constitutional or international public law for officially recognized religious organizations is conducted based on public interest.

text: The processor should assist the controller, where necessary and upon request, in ensuring compliance with the obligations deriving from the carrying out of data protection impact assessments and from prior consultation of the supervisory authority.
rewrite: The processor must help the controller, when needed and upon its request, to meet the obligations arising from conducting data protection impact assessments and from prior consultation with the supervisory authority.

text: Where Member State law applies by virtue of public international law, this Regulation should also apply to a controller not established in the Union, such as in a Member State's diplomatic mission or consular post.
rewrite: Where national law is applicable under public international law, this Regulation shall also extend to controllers not established within the Union, for instance in a diplomatic mission or consular post of a Member State.

text: This Regulation respects and does not prejudice the status under existing constitutional law of churches and religious associations or communities in the Member States, as recognised in Article 17 TFEU.
rewrite: This Regulation upholds and does not undermine the existing constitutional status of churches and religious associations or communities in the Member States, as acknowledged in Article 17 TFEU.

text: When drawing up a code of conduct, or when amending or extending such a code, associations and other bodies representing categories of controllers or processors should consult relevant stakeholders, including data subjects where feasible, and have regard to submissions received and views expressed in response to such consultations.
rewrite: In establishing or revising a code of conduct, associations and groups representing controllers or processors ought to seek input from pertinent stakeholders, including data subjects when possible, and take into account the submissions and perspectives gathered from these consultations.

text: The Commission should adopt immediately applicable implementing acts where available evidence reveals that a third country, a territory or a specified sector within that third country, or an international organisation does not ensure an adequate level of protection, and imperative grounds of urgency so require.
rewrite: The Commission must enact implementing acts with immediate effect when evidence indicates that a third country, territory, specific sector, or international organization fails to provide adequate protection, and urgent circumstances necessitate such action.

text: The application of pseudonymisation to personal data can reduce the risks to the data subjects concerned and help controllers and processors to meet their data-protection obligations. The explicit introduction of ‘pseudony­ misation’ in this Regulation is not intended to preclude any other measures of data protection.
rewrite: The use of pseudonymisation on personal data can lower risks for the relevant data subjects and assist controllers and processors in fulfilling their data-protection duties. The specific inclusion of ‘pseudonymisation’ in this Regulation does not aim to exclude any other data protection measures.

text: In order to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation, the controller or processor should maintain records of processing activities under its responsibility. Each controller and processor should be obliged to cooperate with the supervisory authority and make those records, on request, available to it, so that it might serve for monitoring those processing operations.
rewrite: To show adherence to this Regulation, controllers or processors must keep records of the processing activities they oversee. Every controller and processor is required to assist the supervisory authority and provide these records upon request, enabling the monitoring of such processing operations.

text: A consultation of the supervisory authority should also take place in the course of the preparation of a legislative or regulatory measure which provides for the processing of personal data, in order to ensure compliance of the intended processing with this Regulation and in particular to mitigate the risk involved for the data subject.
rewrite: Consultation with the supervisory authority should also occur during the preparation of any legislative or regulatory measure that involves personal data processing. This is to ensure the intended processing aligns with this Regulation and specifically to reduce the risks to the data subject.

text: Where this Regulation provides for specifications or restrictions of its rules by Member State law, Member States may, as far as necessary for coherence and for making the national provisions comprehensible to the persons to whom they apply, incorporate elements of this Regulation into their national law.
rewrite: When this Regulation allows for specifications or limitations of its provisions through national legislation, Member States may, to the extent needed for consistency and to ensure clarity for those subject to the rules, integrate aspects of this Regulation into their domestic laws.

text: Where personal data are processed for historical research purposes, this Regulation should also apply to that processing. This should also include historical research and research for genealogical purposes, bearing in mind that this Regulation should not apply to deceased persons.
rewrite: When personal data is used for historical research, this Regulation should also govern such processing. This encompasses historical research and genealogical studies, while noting that the Regulation does not apply to deceased individuals.

text: The European Data Protection Supervisor was consulted in accordance with Article 28(2) of Regulation (EC) No 45/2001 and delivered an opinion on 7 March 2012 (1).
rewrite: The European Data Protection Supervisor was consulted as per Article 28(2) of Regulation (EC) No 45/2001 and issued an opinion on 7 March 2012 (1).

text: The independence of supervisory authorities should not mean that the supervisory authorities cannot be subject to control or monitoring mechanisms regarding their financial expenditure or to judicial review.
rewrite: The autonomy of oversight bodies should not imply that they are exempt from controls or monitoring of their financial outlays, nor from judicial scrutiny.

text: For the purpose of consenting to the participation in scientific research activities in clinical trials, the relevant provisions of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council (1) should apply.
rewrite: To consent to participation in scientific research within clinical trials, the applicable rules are those set forth in Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council (1).

text: Profiling is subject to the rules of this Regulation governing the processing of personal data, such as the legal grounds for processing or data protection principles. The European Data Protection Board established by this Regulation (the ‘Board’) should be able to issue guidance in that context.
rewrite: Profiling is governed by this Regulation's rules on personal data processing, including legal bases for processing and data protection principles. The European Data Protection Board created under this Regulation (the 'Board') should have the authority to provide guidance in this area.

text: The main establishment of a controller in the Union should be the place of its central administration in the Union, unless the decisions on the purposes and means of the processing of personal data are taken in another establishment of the controller in the Union, in which case that other establishment should be considered to be
rewrite: The primary establishment of a controller within the Union should be its central administration, unless decisions regarding the purposes and means of processing personal data are made at another establishment of the controller in the Union, in which case that other establishment should be deemed as such.

text: In order to enhance transparency and compliance with this Regulation, the establishment of certification mechanisms and data protection seals and marks should be encouraged, allowing data subjects to quickly assess the level of data protection of relevant products and services.
rewrite: To improve transparency and adherence to this Regulation, the promotion of certification frameworks along with data protection seals and marks should be supported, enabling data subjects to readily evaluate the data protection standards of associated products and services.

text: In the context of the adoption of the Member State law on which the performance of the tasks of the public authority or public body is based and which regulates the specific processing operation or set of operations in question, Member States may deem it necessary to carry out such assessment prior to the processing activities.
rewrite: Within the framework of implementing national legislation that establishes the duties of a public authority or body and governs the specific processing operation or series of operations involved, Member States may consider it essential to conduct this evaluation before initiating the processing activities.

text: Awareness-raising activities by supervisory authorities addressed to the public should include specific measures directed at controllers and processors, including micro, small and medium-sized enterprises, as well as natural persons in particular in the educational context. 4.5.2016 EN Official Journal of the European Union L 119/25
rewrite: Supervisory authorities' public awareness initiatives should incorporate targeted actions for controllers and processors, such as micro, small, and medium-sized businesses, along with individuals, especially within educational settings. 4.5.2016 EN Official Journal of the European Union L 119/25

text: Each supervisory authority should, where appropriate, participate in joint operations with other supervisory authorities. The requested supervisory authority should be obliged to respond to the request within a specified time period.
rewrite: Each supervisory authority ought to, when suitable, engage in joint activities with other supervisory bodies. The authority receiving the request must be required to reply within a designated timeframe.

text: The protection afforded by this Regulation should apply to natural persons, whatever their nationality or place of residence, in relation to the processing of their personal data. This Regulation does not cover the processing of personal data which concerns legal persons and in particular undertakings established as legal persons, including the name and the form of the legal person and the contact details of the legal person.
rewrite: The safeguards established by this Regulation extend to natural persons, irrespective of nationality or residence, regarding the processing of their personal data. This Regulation does not apply to the processing of personal data pertaining to legal persons, notably enterprises constituted as legal persons, encompassing the legal person's name, legal form, and contact information.

text: Natural persons may be associated with online identifiers provided by their devices, applications, tools and protocols, such as internet protocol addresses, cookie identifiers or other identifiers such as radio frequency identification tags. This may leave traces which, in particular when combined with unique identifiers and other information received by the servers, may be used to create profiles of the natural persons and identify them.
rewrite: Individuals can be linked to online identifiers from their devices, applications, tools, and protocols, including IP addresses, cookies, or other markers like RFID tags. These traces, especially when merged with unique identifiers and additional data collected by servers, can be utilized to build profiles of individuals and recognize them.

text: The likelihood and severity of the risk to the rights and freedoms of the data subject should be determined by reference to the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing. Risk should be evaluated on the basis of an objective assessment, by which it is established whether data processing operations involve a risk or a high risk.
rewrite: The probability and impact of risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects must be assessed by considering the nature, scope, context, and purposes of the processing. This evaluation should be based on an objective analysis to determine whether the data processing activities present a risk or a high risk.

text: Genetic data should be defined as personal data relating to the inherited or acquired genetic characteristics of a natural person which result from the analysis of a biological sample from the natural person in question, in particular chromosomal, deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) or ribonucleic acid (RNA) analysis, or from the analysis of another element enabling equivalent information to be obtained.
rewrite: Genetic data must be classified as personal data concerning the inherited or acquired genetic traits of an individual, derived from examining a biological sample from that person. This includes analyses of chromosomes, DNA, or RNA, as well as the examination of other components that yield comparable information.

text: Where a Member State establishes several supervisory authorities, it should establish by law mechanisms for ensuring the effective participation of those supervisory authorities in the consistency mechanism. That Member State should in particular designate the supervisory authority which functions as a single contact point for the effective participation of those authorities in the mechanism, to ensure swift and smooth cooperation with other supervisory authorities, the Board and the Commission.
rewrite: When a Member State sets up multiple supervisory authorities, it must create legal frameworks to guarantee their effective involvement in the consistency mechanism. Specifically, that Member State should appoint one supervisory authority to serve as the central liaison, enabling efficient participation in the mechanism and ensuring prompt and seamless collaboration with other supervisory authorities, the Board, and the Commission.

text: For proceedings against a controller or processor, the plaintiff should have the choice to bring the action before the courts of the Member States where the controller or processor has an establishment or where the data subject resides, unless the controller is a public authority of a Member State acting in the exercise of its public powers.
rewrite: In legal actions involving a controller or processor, the claimant may opt to file the case in the courts of the Member States where the controller or processor operates an establishment or where the data subject is domiciled, except when the controller is a public authority of a Member State exercising its public powers.

text: Where this Regulation does not harmonise administrative penalties or where necessary in other cases, for example in cases of serious infringements of this Regulation, Member States should implement a system which provides for effective, proportionate and dissuasive penalties. The nature of such penalties, criminal or adminis­ trative, should be determined by Member State law.
rewrite: Where this Regulation does not establish uniform administrative penalties or where required in other instances, such as for serious breaches of this Regulation, Member States ought to adopt a system that ensures penalties are effective, proportionate, and dissuasive. The type of these penalties, whether criminal or administrative, should be defined by the laws of each Member State.

text: There may be an urgent need to act in order to protect the rights and freedoms of data subjects, in particular when the danger exists that the enforcement of a right of a data subject could be considerably impeded. A supervisory authority should therefore be able to adopt duly justified provisional measures on its territory with a specified period of validity which should not exceed three months.
rewrite: When there is an urgent need to safeguard the rights and freedoms of data subjects, especially if enforcing such rights might be significantly hindered, immediate action may be required. Consequently, a supervisory authority ought to have the power to implement properly justified provisional measures within its jurisdiction, valid for a specified duration not exceeding three months.

text: There are circumstances under which it may be reasonable and economical for the subject of a data protection impact assessment to be broader than a single project, for example where public authorities or bodies intend to establish a common application or processing platform or where several controllers plan to introduce a common application or processing environment across an industry sector or segment or for a widely used horizontal activity.
rewrite: In certain situations, it can be both reasonable and cost-effective for a data protection impact assessment to cover a scope wider than just one project. This applies, for instance, when public authorities or organizations aim to set up a shared application or processing platform, or when multiple controllers intend to implement a common application or processing framework across an industry sector, segment, or for a widely adopted horizontal activity.

text: The supervisory authorities should assist each other in performing their tasks and provide mutual assistance, so as to ensure the consistent application and enforcement of this Regulation in the internal market. A supervisory authority requesting mutual assistance may adopt a provisional measure if it receives no response to a request for mutual assistance within one month of the receipt of that request by the other supervisory authority.
rewrite: Supervisory authorities must support one another in carrying out their duties and offer mutual assistance to guarantee uniform application and enforcement of this Regulation within the internal market. If a supervisory authority receives no reply to a request for mutual assistance within one month after the other authority has received it, the requesting authority may implement a provisional measure.

text: Children merit specific protection with regard to their personal data, as they may be less aware of the risks, consequences and safeguards concerned and their rights in relation to the processing of personal data. Such specific protection should, in particular, apply to the use of personal data of children for the purposes of marketing or creating personality or user profiles and the collection of personal data with regard to children when using services offered directly to a child. The consent of the holder of parental responsibility should not be necessary in the context of preventive or counselling services offered directly to a child.
rewrite: Children deserve particular protection concerning their personal data, as they might be less conscious of the associated risks, outcomes, safeguards, and their rights regarding data processing. This special protection should especially cover using children's personal data for marketing or building personality or user profiles, and gathering such data when services are directly offered to a child. Parental consent should not be required for preventive or advisory services provided directly to a child.

text: This Regulation does not apply to issues of protection of fundamental rights and freedoms or the free flow of personal data related to activities which fall outside the scope of Union law, such as activities concerning national security. This Regulation does not apply to the processing of personal data by the Member States when carrying out activities in relation to the common foreign and security policy of the Union.
rewrite: This Regulation does not apply to matters concerning the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms or the free movement of personal data in activities outside the scope of Union law, including those pertaining to national security. It also does not apply to the processing of personal data by Member States when undertaking activities related to the Union’s common foreign and security policy.

text: Where in the course of electoral activities, the operation of the democratic system in a Member State requires that political parties compile personal data on people's political opinions, the processing of such data may be permitted for reasons of public interest, provided that appropriate safeguards are established.
rewrite: In the context of electoral processes, when the functioning of a democratic system within a Member State necessitates that political parties collect personal data regarding individuals' political views, such processing may be allowed on grounds of public interest, given that suitable protective measures are implemented.

text: This Regulation is without prejudice to the application of Directive 2000/31/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council (2), in particular of the liability rules of intermediary service providers in Articles 12 to 15 of that Directive. That Directive seeks to contribute to the proper functioning of the internal market by ensuring the free movement of information society services between Member States.
rewrite: This Regulation does not affect the application of Directive 2000/31/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council (2), notably the liability provisions for intermediary service providers under Articles 12 to 15 of that Directive. The aim of that Directive is to support the proper functioning of the internal market by guaranteeing the free movement of information society services among Member States.

text: Those developments require a strong and more coherent data protection framework in the Union, backed by strong enforcement, given the importance of creating the trust that will allow the digital economy to develop across the internal market. Natural persons should have control of their own personal data. Legal and practical certainty for natural persons, economic operators and public authorities should be enhanced.
rewrite: These advancements necessitate a robust and more unified data protection framework within the Union, supported by rigorous enforcement, due to the critical need to foster the trust essential for the digital economy to flourish throughout the internal market. Individuals must be empowered to manage their personal data. Legal and practical clarity for individuals, businesses, and public authorities should be strengthened.

text: Each supervisory authority should be provided with the financial and human resources, premises and infrastructure necessary for the effective performance of their tasks, including those related to mutual assistance and cooperation with other supervisory authorities throughout the Union. Each supervisory authority should have a separate, public annual budget, which may be part of the overall state or national budget.
rewrite: Every supervisory authority must be allocated the financial and human resources, facilities, and infrastructure required to effectively carry out its duties, including those involving mutual assistance and cooperation with other supervisory authorities across the Union. Each authority should also maintain an independent, publicly accessible annual budget, which may be integrated into the broader state or national budget.

text: Directive (EU) 2016/680 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data by competent authorities for the purposes of prevention, investigation, detection or prosecution of criminal offences or the execution of criminal penalties, and the free movement of such data and repealing Council Framework Decision 2008/977/JHA (see page 89 of this Official Journal).
rewrite: Directive (EU) 2016/680, adopted by the European Parliament and Council on 27 April 2016, concerns safeguarding natural persons in relation to personal data processing by competent authorities for preventing, investigating, detecting, or prosecuting criminal offences or enforcing criminal penalties, and on the free movement of such data, while repealing Council Framework Decision 2008/977/JHA (refer to page 89 of this Official Journal).

text: The establishment of supervisory authorities in Member States, empowered to perform their tasks and exercise their powers with complete independence, is an essential component of the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of their personal data. Member States should be able to establish more than one supervisory authority, to reflect their constitutional, organisational and administrative structure.
rewrite: The creation of supervisory bodies in Member States, granted the authority to carry out their duties and wield their powers with full autonomy, is a fundamental element in safeguarding individuals concerning the handling of their personal data. Member States ought to have the capacity to set up multiple supervisory authorities, in order to align with their constitutional, organizational, and administrative frameworks.

text: In such cases, a data protection impact assessment should be carried out by the controller prior to the processing in order to assess the particular likelihood and severity of the high risk, taking into account the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing and the sources of the risk. That impact assessment should include, in particular, the measures, safeguards and mechanisms envisaged for mitigating that risk, ensuring the protection of personal data and demonstrating compliance with this Regulation.
rewrite: In such instances, a data protection impact assessment must be conducted by the controller before processing to evaluate the specific likelihood and severity of high risk, considering the processing's nature, scope, context, purposes, and risk sources. This assessment should specifically encompass the measures, safeguards, and mechanisms planned to mitigate the risk, protect personal data, and demonstrate adherence to this Regulation.

text: The protection of the rights and freedoms of data subjects as well as the responsibility and liability of controllers and processors, also in relation to the monitoring by and measures of supervisory authorities, requires a clear allocation of the responsibilities under this Regulation, including where a controller determines the purposes and means of the processing jointly with other controllers or where a processing operation is carried out on behalf of a controller.
rewrite: Safeguarding the rights and freedoms of data subjects, along with the accountability and obligations of controllers and processors—including in the context of oversight by supervisory authorities and their enforcement actions—necessitates a precise delineation of duties under this Regulation. This applies both when controllers jointly determine the purposes and means of processing with others and when processing is conducted on a controller’s behalf.

text: Where personal data might lawfully be processed because processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller, or on grounds of the legitimate interests of a controller or a third party, a data subject should, nevertheless, be entitled to object to the processing of any personal data relating to his or her particular situation. It should be for the controller to demonstrate that its compelling legitimate interest overrides the interests or the fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject.
rewrite: Even when personal data processing is legally permitted for public interest tasks, official authority, or legitimate interests of the controller or a third party, the data subject retains the right to object based on their specific circumstances. The controller must then prove that its compelling legitimate interest outweighs the data subject’s interests, fundamental rights, and freedoms.

text: The Board should be assisted by a secretariat provided by the European Data Protection Supervisor. The staff of the European Data Protection Supervisor involved in carrying out the tasks conferred on the Board by this Regulation should perform its tasks exclusively under the instructions of, and report to, the Chair of the Board.
rewrite: The Board must be supported by a secretariat supplied by the European Data Protection Supervisor. Personnel from the European Data Protection Supervisor assigned to the Board's duties under this Regulation shall carry out their functions solely under the direction of and report directly to the Board's Chair.

text: A group of undertakings should cover a controlling undertaking and its controlled undertakings, whereby the controlling undertaking should be the undertaking which can exert a dominant influence over the other undertakings by virtue, for example, of ownership, financial participation or the rules which govern it or the power to have personal data protection rules implemented. An undertaking which controls the processing of personal data in undertakings affiliated to it should be regarded, together with those undertakings, as a group of undertakings.
rewrite: A group of undertakings should comprise a controlling undertaking and the undertakings it controls. The controlling undertaking is one that can exercise a dominant influence over others, for instance through ownership, financial involvement, its governing rules, or the authority to enforce personal data protection rules. An undertaking that oversees personal data processing within its affiliated undertakings, together with those affiliates, should be considered a group of undertakings.

text: The economic and social integration resulting from the functioning of the internal market has led to a substantial increase in cross-border flows of personal data. The exchange of personal data between public and private actors, including natural persons, associations and undertakings across the Union has increased. National authorities in the Member States are being called upon by Union law to cooperate and exchange personal data so as to be able to perform their duties or carry out tasks on behalf of an authority in another Member State.
rewrite: The operation of the internal market has fostered economic and social integration, significantly boosting cross-border transfers of personal data. There is a growing exchange of such data among public and private entities, including individuals, associations, and businesses throughout the Union. Under Union law, national authorities in Member States are required to collaborate and share personal data to fulfill their responsibilities or execute tasks on behalf of counterparts in other Member States.

text: In order for processing to be lawful, personal data should be processed on the basis of the consent of the data subject concerned or some other legitimate basis, laid down by law, either in this Regulation or in other Union or L 119/8 EN Official Journal of the European Union 4.5.2016 Member State law as referred to in this Regulation, including the necessity for compliance with the legal obligation to which the controller is subject or the necessity for the performance of a contract to which the data subject is party or in order to take steps at the request of the data subject prior to entering into a contract.
rewrite: For lawful processing, personal data must be processed based on the data subject's consent or another lawful basis established by law, whether under this Regulation or other Union or Member State law referenced herein. This includes the need to comply with a legal obligation binding the controller, to perform a contract involving the data subject, or to take pre-contractual measures at the data subject's request.

text: The rules on the lead supervisory authority and the one-stop-shop mechanism should not apply where the processing is carried out by public authorities or private bodies in the public interest. In such cases the only supervisory authority competent to exercise the powers conferred to it in accordance with this Regulation should be the supervisory authority of the Member State where the public authority or private body is established.
rewrite: The provisions concerning the lead supervisory authority and the one-stop-shop mechanism are not applicable when processing is conducted by public authorities or private entities acting in the public interest. In these instances, the sole supervisory authority with the competence to utilize the powers granted under this Regulation should be that of the Member State in which the public authority or private entity is established.

text: A group of undertakings, or a group of enterprises engaged in a joint economic activity, should be able to make use of approved binding corporate rules for its international transfers from the Union to organisations within the same group of undertakings, or group of enterprises engaged in a joint economic activity, provided that such corporate rules include all essential principles and enforceable rights to ensure appropriate safeguards for transfers or categories of transfers of personal data.
rewrite: A group of undertakings, or enterprises jointly engaged in economic activity, should be permitted to utilize approved binding corporate rules for transferring data internationally from the Union to entities within the same corporate group, or group of enterprises involved in joint economic activity. This is conditional on such corporate rules encompassing all essential principles and enforceable rights to guarantee appropriate safeguards for transfers or categories of transfers of personal data.

text: Where this Regulation refers to a legal basis or a legislative measure, this does not necessarily require a legislative act adopted by a parliament, without prejudice to requirements pursuant to the constitutional order of the Member State concerned. However, such a legal basis or legislative measure should be clear and precise and its application should be foreseeable to persons subject to it, in accordance with the case-law of the Court of Justice of the European Union (the ‘Court of Justice’) and the European Court of Human Rights.
rewrite: When this Regulation mentions a legal basis or legislative measure, it does not always imply an act passed by a parliament, subject to the constitutional rules of the relevant Member State. Nonetheless, any such legal basis or legislative measure must be clear and precise, and its implementation should be predictable for those it affects, following the jurisprudence of the Court of Justice of the European Union and the European Court of Human Rights.

text: The protection of natural persons in relation to the processing of personal data is a fundamental right. Article 8(1) of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (the ‘Charter’) and Article 16(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) provide that everyone has the right to the protection of personal data concerning him or her.
rewrite: Safeguarding natural persons regarding the processing of their personal data constitutes a fundamental right. According to Article 8(1) of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (the ‘Charter’) and Article 16(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), every individual holds the right to protection of personal data pertaining to them.

text: In any case, where the Commission has taken no decision on the adequate level of data protection in a third country, the controller or processor should make use of solutions that provide data subjects with enforceable and effective rights as regards the processing of their data in the Union once those data have been transferred so that that they will continue to benefit from fundamental rights and safeguards. L 119/22 EN Official Journal of the European Union 4.5.2016
rewrite: In situations where the Commission has not determined that a third country ensures an adequate level of data protection, the controller or processor must implement measures that grant data subjects enforceable and effective rights regarding the processing of their data within the Union after transfer, ensuring they retain fundamental rights and protections. L 119/22 EN Official Journal of the European Union 4.5.2016

text: To strengthen the right to be forgotten in the online environment, the right to erasure should also be extended in such a way that a controller who has made the personal data public should be obliged to inform the controllers which are processing such personal data to erase any links to, or copies or replications of those personal data. In doing so, that controller should take reasonable steps, taking into account available technology and the means available to the controller, including technical measures, to inform the controllers which are processing the personal data of the data subject's request.
rewrite: To enhance the right to be forgotten online, the right to erasure should be broadened so that a controller who has disclosed personal data must notify other controllers processing that data to delete any links, copies, or replications. In this process, the controller should take reasonable actions, considering available technology and resources, such as technical measures, to inform the relevant controllers of the data subject's erasure request.

text: As regards the powers of the supervisory authorities to obtain from the controller or processor access to personal data and access to their premises, Member States may adopt by law, within the limits of this Regulation, specific rules in order to safeguard the professional or other equivalent secrecy obligations, in so far as necessary to reconcile the right to the protection of personal data with an obligation of professional secrecy. This is without prejudice to existing Member State obligations to adopt rules on professional secrecy where required by Union law.
rewrite: Concerning the authority of supervisory bodies to access personal data and premises from controllers or processors, Member States may establish specific legal provisions within this Regulation's boundaries. These rules aim to protect professional or similar confidentiality duties, as needed to balance personal data protection rights with professional secrecy obligations. This does not affect current Member State requirements to enact professional secrecy rules under Union law mandates.

text: Methods by which to restrict the processing of personal data could include, inter alia, temporarily moving the selected data to another processing system, making the selected personal data unavailable to users, or temporarily removing published data from a website. In automated filing systems, the restriction of processing should in principle be ensured by technical means in such a manner that the personal data are not subject to further processing operations and cannot be changed. The fact that the processing of personal data is restricted should be clearly indicated in the system.
rewrite: Methods to limit the processing of personal data may involve, among other things, temporarily transferring chosen data to a different processing system, rendering selected personal data inaccessible to users, or provisionally taking down published data from a website. In automated filing systems, restricting processing should generally be secured through technical measures so that the personal data undergo no additional processing and remain unalterable. It should be clearly marked within the system that the processing of personal data is restricted.

text: Effective protection of personal data throughout the Union requires the strengthening and setting out in detail of the rights of data subjects and the obligations of those who process and determine the processing of personal data, as well as equivalent powers for monitoring and ensuring compliance with the rules for the protection of personal data and equivalent sanctions for infringements in the Member States.
rewrite: To ensure robust personal data protection across the Union, it is essential to enhance and clearly define the rights of individuals, along with the duties of those handling and controlling personal data processing. This includes establishing uniform supervisory authority and enforcement measures, as well as consistent penalties for violations in all Member States.

text: The decision should be agreed jointly by the lead supervisory authority and the supervisory authorities concerned and should be directed towards the main or single establishment of the controller or processor and be binding on the controller and processor. The controller or processor should take the necessary measures to ensure compliance with this Regulation and the implementation of the decision notified by the lead supervisory authority to the main establishment of the controller or processor as regards the processing activities in the Union.
rewrite: The decision must be jointly agreed upon by the lead supervisory authority and the concerned supervisory authorities. It should be addressed to the controller's or processor's main or single establishment and be binding on them. The controller or processor is required to take necessary measures to comply with this Regulation and to implement the decision, which is notified by the lead supervisory authority to their main establishment, regarding processing activities within the Union.

text: Controllers that are part of a group of undertakings or institutions affiliated to a central body may have a legitimate interest in transmitting personal data within the group of undertakings for internal administrative purposes, including the processing of clients' or employees' personal data. The general principles for the transfer of personal data, within a group of undertakings, to an undertaking located in a third country remain unaffected.
rewrite: Controllers that belong to a group of undertakings or institutions linked to a central body may have a legitimate interest in sharing personal data within the group for internal administrative purposes, such as handling personal data of clients or employees. The fundamental principles for transferring personal data within a group of undertakings to an entity in a third country remain unchanged.

text: It is often not possible to fully identify the purpose of personal data processing for scientific research purposes at the time of data collection. Therefore, data subjects should be allowed to give their consent to certain areas of scientific research when in keeping with recognised ethical standards for scientific research. Data subjects should have the opportunity to give their consent only to certain areas of research or parts of research projects to the extent allowed by the intended purpose.
rewrite: Frequently, it is not feasible to precisely determine the purpose of processing personal data for scientific research at the moment of collection. Consequently, data subjects ought to be permitted to provide consent for specific domains of scientific research, provided these align with established ethical norms in the field. They should also have the option to consent solely to particular research areas or segments of projects, within the limits set by the intended objectives.

text: The supervisory authorities should monitor the application of the provisions pursuant to this Regulation and contribute to its consistent application throughout the Union, in order to protect natural persons in relation to the processing of their personal data and to facilitate the free flow of personal data within the internal market. For that purpose, the supervisory authorities should cooperate with each other and with the Commission, without the need for any agreement between Member States on the provision of mutual assistance or on such cooperation.
rewrite: The supervisory authorities must oversee the implementation of the provisions under this Regulation and help ensure its uniform application across the Union. This is to safeguard individuals regarding the processing of their personal data and to promote the free movement of personal data within the internal market. To achieve this, the supervisory authorities should collaborate with one another and with the Commission, without requiring any agreement among Member States on mutual assistance or such cooperation.

text: The processing of personal data of data subjects who are in the Union by a controller or processor not established in the Union should also be subject to this Regulation when it is related to the monitoring of the behaviour of such data subjects in so far as their behaviour takes place within the Union. In order to determine whether a processing activity can be considered to monitor the behaviour of data subjects, it should be ascertained whether natural persons are tracked on the internet including potential subsequent use of personal data processing techniques which consist of profiling a natural person, particularly in order to take decisions concerning her or him or for analysing or predicting her or his personal preferences, behaviours and attitudes.
rewrite: The processing of personal data belonging to individuals in the Union by a controller or processor located outside the Union must also comply with this Regulation if it involves monitoring those individuals’ behavior within the Union. To assess whether a processing activity constitutes monitoring, it should be determined if natural persons are tracked online, including through subsequent use of techniques like profiling. This applies especially when such processing aims to make decisions about an individual or to analyze or predict their personal preferences, behaviors, and attitudes.

text: The principles of, and rules on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of their personal data should, whatever their nationality or residence, respect their fundamental rights and freedoms, in particular their right to the protection of personal data. This Regulation is intended to contribute to the accomplishment of an area of freedom, security and justice and of an economic union, to economic and social progress, to the strengthening and the convergence of the economies within the internal market, and to the well-being of natural persons.
rewrite: The principles and rules protecting natural persons concerning the processing of their personal data must, regardless of nationality or residence, uphold their fundamental rights and freedoms, especially the right to personal data protection. This Regulation aims to support the establishment of an area of freedom, security, and justice, along with an economic union, to advance economic and social progress, enhance and align economies in the internal market, and promote the well-being of natural persons.

text: In order to ensure uniform conditions for the implementation of this Regulation, implementing powers should be conferred on the Commission when provided for by this Regulation. Those powers should be exercised in accordance with Regulation (EU) No 182/2011. In that context, the Commission should consider specific measures for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises.
rewrite: To guarantee consistent application of this Regulation, implementing authority should be delegated to the Commission as stipulated herein. Such powers must be executed in compliance with Regulation (EU) No 182/2011. Within this framework, the Commission ought to evaluate tailored provisions for micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises.

text: Where specific rules on jurisdiction are contained in this Regulation, in particular as regards proceedings seeking a judicial remedy including compensation, against a controller or processor, general jurisdiction rules such as those of Regulation (EU) No 1215/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council (1) should not prejudice the application of such specific rules.
rewrite: Where this Regulation includes particular provisions on jurisdiction, especially concerning legal actions that seek judicial remedies such as compensation against a controller or processor, broader jurisdictional frameworks like those under Regulation (EU) No 1215/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council (1) must not undermine the implementation of these specific rules.

text: Associations or other bodies representing categories of controllers or processors should be encouraged to draw up codes of conduct, within the limits of this Regulation, so as to facilitate the effective application of this Regulation, taking account of the specific characteristics of the processing carried out in certain sectors and the specific needs of micro, small and medium enterprises. In particular, such codes of conduct could calibrate the obligations of controllers and processors, taking into account the risk likely to result from the processing for the rights and freedoms of natural persons.
rewrite: Associations or groups representing types of controllers or processors should be encouraged to develop codes of conduct, within the boundaries of this Regulation, to aid in the effective implementation of this Regulation. These codes should consider the particular features of processing in specific sectors and the distinct requirements of micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises. Specifically, such codes could adjust the responsibilities of controllers and processors, accounting for the potential risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals arising from the processing.

text: In setting detailed rules concerning the format and procedures applicable to the notification of personal data breaches, due consideration should be given to the circumstances of that breach, including whether or not personal data had been protected by appropriate technical protection measures, effectively limiting the likelihood of identity fraud or other forms of misuse. Moreover, such rules and procedures should take into account the legitimate interests of law-enforcement authorities where early disclosure could unnecessarily hamper the investi­ gation of the circumstances of a personal data breach.
rewrite: When establishing specific regulations on the format and procedures for reporting personal data breaches, careful attention must be paid to the details of the incident, such as whether the data was secured by suitable technical safeguards that effectively reduce the risk of identity theft or similar abuses. Additionally, these regulations and procedures should account for the valid concerns of law enforcement, in cases where premature disclosure might unduly interfere with investigating the breach's circumstances.

text: This Regulation is without prejudice to international agreements concluded between the Union and third countries regulating the transfer of personal data including appropriate safeguards for the data subjects. Member States may conclude international agreements which involve the transfer of personal data to third countries or in­ ternational organisations, as far as such agreements do not affect this Regulation or any other provisions of Union law and include an appropriate level of protection for the fundamental rights of the data subjects.
rewrite: This Regulation does not affect international agreements between the Union and third countries that govern personal data transfers and include adequate safeguards for data subjects. Member States may enter into international agreements involving the transfer of personal data to third countries or international organisations, provided such agreements do not contravene this Regulation or other Union law and ensure an appropriate level of protection for the fundamental rights of the data subjects.

text: In order to prevent creating a serious risk of circumvention, the protection of natural persons should be technolo­ gically neutral and should not depend on the techniques used. The protection of natural persons should apply to the processing of personal data by automated means, as well as to manual processing, if the personal data are contained or are intended to be contained in a filing system. Files or sets of files, as well as their cover pages, which are not structured according to specific criteria should not fall within the scope of this Regulation.
rewrite: To avoid creating a significant risk of circumvention, the protection of individuals should be technology-neutral and independent of the methods employed. Such protection must cover both automated and manual processing of personal data, provided the data are part of or intended for a filing system. However, files or sets of files, including their covers, that lack organization based on specific criteria should be excluded from this Regulation’s scope.

text: In order to create incentives to apply pseudonymisation when processing personal data, measures of pseudonymi­ sation should, whilst allowing general analysis, be possible within the same controller when that controller has taken technical and organisational measures necessary to ensure, for the processing concerned, that this Regulation is implemented, and that additional information for attributing the personal data to a specific data subject is kept separately. The controller processing the personal data should indicate the authorised persons within the same controller. L 119/6 EN Official Journal of the European Union 4.5.2016
rewrite: To encourage the use of pseudonymisation in personal data processing, pseudonymisation measures should be feasible within a single controller, provided that the controller has implemented appropriate technical and organisational safeguards to ensure compliance with this Regulation for the relevant processing, and that additional information linking the data to an identifiable individual is stored separately. The controller handling the data must specify which individuals within the same controller are authorised. L 119/6 EN Official Journal of the European Union 4.5.2016

text: The confidential information which the Union and national statistical authorities collect for the production of official European and official national statistics should be protected. European statistics should be developed, produced and disseminated in accordance with the statistical principles as set out in Article 338(2) TFEU, while national statistics should also comply with Member State law. Regulation (EC) No 223/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council (2) provides further specifications on statistical confidentiality for European statistics.
rewrite: The confidential data gathered by the Union and national statistical bodies for creating official European and national statistics must be safeguarded. European statistics should be developed, produced, and distributed in line with the statistical principles established in Article 338(2) TFEU, whereas national statistics must also adhere to the laws of Member States. Further details on statistical confidentiality for European statistics are outlined in Regulation (EC) No 223/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council (2).

text: If the personal data processed by a controller do not permit the controller to identify a natural person, the data controller should not be obliged to acquire additional information in order to identify the data subject for the sole purpose of complying with any provision of this Regulation. However, the controller should not refuse to take additional information provided by the data subject in order to support the exercise of his or her rights. Identification should include the digital identification of a data subject, for example through authentication mechanism such as the same credentials, used by the data subject to log-in to the on-line service offered by the data controller.
rewrite: When a controller processes personal data that does not enable the identification of a natural person, the controller should not be required to obtain further information solely to identify the data subject for compliance with this Regulation. Nonetheless, the controller should not decline to accept additional details provided by the data subject to facilitate the exercise of their rights. Identification should encompass the digital identification of a data subject, for instance via authentication methods like the same credentials used by the data subject to access the online service provided by the controller.

text: In order to ensure the consistent application of this Regulation throughout the Union, a consistency mechanism for cooperation between the supervisory authorities should be established. That mechanism should in particular apply where a supervisory authority intends to adopt a measure intended to produce legal effects as regards processing operations which substantially affect a significant number of data subjects in several Member States. It should also apply where any supervisory authority concerned or the Commission requests that such matter should be handled in the consistency mechanism. That mechanism should be without prejudice to any measures that the Commission may take in the exercise of its powers under the Treaties.
rewrite: To guarantee uniform implementation of this Regulation across the Union, a consistency mechanism for cooperation among supervisory authorities must be established. This mechanism should specifically be used when a supervisory authority plans to implement a measure with legal effects concerning processing activities that significantly impact a substantial number of data subjects in multiple Member States. It should also be invoked when any involved supervisory authority or the Commission requests that the issue be addressed through the consistency mechanism. This mechanism does not affect any actions the Commission may undertake using its powers under the Treaties.

text: Rapid technological developments and globalisation have brought new challenges for the protection of personal data. The scale of the collection and sharing of personal data has increased significantly. Technology allows both private companies and public authorities to make use of personal data on an unprecedented scale in order to pursue their activities. Natural persons increasingly make personal information available publicly and globally. Technology has transformed both the economy and social life, and should further facilitate the free flow of personal data within the Union and the transfer to third countries and international organisations, while ensuring a high level of the protection of personal data.
rewrite: Rapid technological progress and globalization present fresh challenges for safeguarding personal data. The extent of data collection and sharing has grown substantially. Technology enables both private firms and public bodies to utilize personal data on an unprecedented scale for their operations. Individuals are increasingly sharing personal information publicly and worldwide. Technology has reshaped the economy and social interactions, and should also promote the free movement of personal data within the Union and its transfer to third countries and international organizations, while maintaining a high standard of data protection.

text: ‘personal data’ means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (‘data subject’); an identifiable natural person is one who can be identified, directly or indirectly, in particular by reference to an identifier such as a name, an identification number, location data, an online identifier or to one or more factors specific to the physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social identity of that natural person;
rewrite: "Personal data" refers to any information concerning an identified or identifiable natural person (the "data subject"). An identifiable natural person is someone who can be recognized, either directly or indirectly, especially through identifiers like a name, an ID number, location details, an online identifier, or one or more elements relating to the physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural, or social identity of that individual.

text: The Commission may decide with effect for the entire Union that a third country, a territory or specified sector within a third country, or an international organisation, offers an adequate level of data protection, thus providing legal certainty and uniformity throughout the Union as regards the third country or international organisation which is considered to provide such level of protection. In such cases, transfers of personal data to that third country or international organisation may take place without the need to obtain any further authoris­ ation. The Commission may also decide, having given notice and a full statement setting out the reasons to the third country or international organisation, to revoke such a decision.
rewrite: The Commission can determine that a third country, territory, specific sector within a third country, or an international organization ensures an adequate level of data protection, applicable across the entire Union. This establishes legal certainty and consistency throughout the Union regarding the third country or international organization deemed to provide such protection. Consequently, transfers of personal data to that third country or international organization may proceed without requiring additional authorization. The Commission may also revoke such a decision, after providing notice and a comprehensive explanation of the reasons to the third country or international organization.

text: However, it is not necessary to impose the obligation to provide information where the data subject already possesses the information, where the recording or disclosure of the personal data is expressly laid down by law or where the provision of information to the data subject proves to be impossible or would involve a dispropor­ tionate effort. The latter could in particular be the case where processing is carried out for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes. In that regard, the number of data subjects, the age of the data and any appropriate safeguards adopted should be taken into consideration.
rewrite: Nevertheless, the duty to furnish information may be waived if the data subject already has the information, if the recording or disclosure of personal data is explicitly mandated by law, or if providing such information to the data subject is unfeasible or would entail a disproportionate burden. This may especially apply when processing is conducted for archiving in the public interest, scientific or historical research, or statistical purposes. In such cases, factors like the number of data subjects, the age of the data, and any suitable safeguards implemented should be considered.

text: Member States should be able to lay down the rules on criminal penalties for infringements of this Regulation, including for infringements of national rules adopted pursuant to and within the limits of this Regulation. Those criminal penalties may also allow for the deprivation of the profits obtained through infringements of this Regulation. However, the imposition of criminal penalties for infringements of such national rules and of administrative penalties should not lead to a breach of the principle of ne bis in idem, as interpreted by the Court of Justice.
rewrite: Member States should have the authority to establish criminal penalties for violations of this Regulation, including for breaches of national rules enacted in accordance with and within the scope of this Regulation. These criminal penalties may also provide for the confiscation of gains acquired from infringements of this Regulation. Nevertheless, imposing criminal penalties for breaches of such national rules, along with administrative penalties, must not result in a violation of the ne bis in idem principle, as construed by the Court of Justice.

text: Any processing of personal data in the context of the activities of an establishment of a controller or a processor in the Union should be carried out in accordance with this Regulation, regardless of whether the processing itself takes place within the Union. Establishment implies the effective and real exercise of activity through stable arrangements. The legal form of such arrangements, whether through a branch or a subsidiary with a legal personality, is not the determining factor in that respect.
rewrite: Any handling of personal data within the activities of an establishment of a controller or processor in the Union must comply with this Regulation, irrespective of whether the processing occurs within the Union. Establishment entails the effective and genuine conduct of activities through stable arrangements. The legal structure of these arrangements, be it a branch or a legally recognized subsidiary, is not the decisive element in this regard.

text: Where personal data are processed for the purposes of direct marketing, the data subject should have the right to object to such processing, including profiling to the extent that it is related to such direct marketing, whether with regard to initial or further processing, at any time and free of charge. That right should be explicitly brought to the attention of the data subject and presented clearly and separately from any other information. L 119/14 EN Official Journal of the European Union 4.5.2016
rewrite: When personal data is used for direct marketing purposes, the data subject must have the right to object to this processing at any time and without charge. This includes any profiling connected to such marketing, whether during initial or subsequent processing. This right must be clearly and separately communicated to the data subject, distinct from any other information. L 119/14 EN Official Journal of the European Union 4.5.2016

text: In order to ensure that consent is freely given, consent should not provide a valid legal ground for the processing of personal data in a specific case where there is a clear imbalance between the data subject and the controller, in particular where the controller is a public authority and it is therefore unlikely that consent was freely given in all the circumstances of that specific situation. Consent is presumed not to be freely given if it does not allow separate consent to be given to different personal data processing operations despite it being appropriate in the individual case, or if the performance of a contract, including the provision of a service, is dependent on the consent despite such consent not being necessary for such performance.
rewrite: To guarantee that consent is freely provided, it should not serve as a lawful basis for processing personal data when a significant power imbalance exists between the data subject and the controller. This is especially relevant if the controller is a public authority, making it improbable that consent was given freely under the specific circumstances. Consent is considered not freely given if it fails to permit separate consent for distinct processing activities where appropriate, or if fulfilling a contract or service is made conditional on consent that is not required for that performance.

text: The application of such mechanism should be a condition for the lawfulness of a measure intended to produce legal effects by a supervisory authority in those cases where its application is mandatory. In other cases of cross- border relevance, the cooperation mechanism between the lead supervisory authority and supervisory authorities concerned should be applied and mutual assistance and joint operations might be carried out between the supervisory authorities concerned on a bilateral or multilateral basis without triggering the consistency mechanism.
rewrite: The use of this mechanism must be a prerequisite for the legality of any action by a supervisory authority that aims to create legal effects, wherever its application is required. In other instances with cross-border implications, the cooperation framework between the lead supervisory authority and the relevant supervisory authorities should be employed, and mutual support or joint activities may be conducted among the concerned supervisory authorities bilaterally or multilaterally, without activating the consistency mechanism.

text: In order to enhance compliance with this Regulation where processing operations are likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller should be responsible for the carrying-out of a data protection impact assessment to evaluate, in particular, the origin, nature, particularity and severity of that risk. The outcome of the assessment should be taken into account when determining the appropriate measures to be taken in order to demonstrate that the processing of personal data complies with this Regulation. Where a data-protection impact assessment indicates that processing operations involve a high risk which the controller cannot mitigate by appropriate measures in terms of available technology and costs of implementation, a consultation of the supervisory authority should take place prior to the processing.
rewrite: To improve adherence to this Regulation when processing activities may pose a significant risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, the controller must conduct a data protection impact assessment. This assessment should specifically examine the source, nature, distinctiveness, and seriousness of the risk. The findings from this evaluation must inform the selection of suitable measures to show that personal data processing aligns with this Regulation. If the impact assessment reveals a high risk that the controller cannot sufficiently reduce through feasible technological and cost-effective measures, consultation with the supervisory authority is required before proceeding with the processing.

text: It should be ascertained whether all appropriate technological protection and organisational measures have been implemented to establish immediately whether a personal data breach has taken place and to inform promptly the supervisory authority and the data subject. The fact that the notification was made without undue delay should be established taking into account in particular the nature and gravity of the personal data breach and its consequences and adverse effects for the data subject. Such notification may result in an intervention of the supervisory authority in accordance with its tasks and powers laid down in this Regulation.
rewrite: It must be determined whether all suitable technological safeguards and organizational steps have been taken to quickly identify any personal data breach and to notify the supervisory authority and the affected individual without delay. Whether the notification was provided promptly should be assessed, particularly considering the type and severity of the breach, along with its consequences and negative impacts on the data subject. This notification could lead to action by the supervisory authority, as permitted by its duties and authority under this Regulation.

text: The lead authority should be competent to adopt binding decisions regarding measures applying the powers conferred on it in accordance with this Regulation. In its capacity as lead authority, the supervisory authority should closely involve and coordinate the supervisory authorities concerned in the decision-making process. Where the decision is to reject the complaint by the data subject in whole or in part, that decision should be adopted by the supervisory authority with which the complaint has been lodged.
rewrite: The lead authority must be capable of issuing binding decisions that utilize the powers granted to it under this Regulation. As the lead authority, it should actively engage and coordinate with the relevant supervisory authorities throughout the decision-making process. If the decision involves rejecting a data subject's complaint, either fully or partially, that decision should be made by the supervisory authority to which the complaint was originally submitted.

text: Apart from the international commitments the third country or international organisation has entered into, the Commission should take account of obligations arising from the third country's or international organisation's participation in multilateral or regional systems in particular in relation to the protection of personal data, as well as the implementation of such obligations. In particular, the third country's accession to the Council of Europe Convention of 28 January 1981 for the Protection of Individuals with regard to the Automatic Processing of Personal Data and its Additional Protocol should be taken into account. The Commission should consult the Board when assessing the level of protection in third countries or international organisations.
rewrite: Beyond the international agreements a third country or international organisation has undertaken, the Commission should consider duties stemming from its involvement in multilateral or regional frameworks, especially concerning personal data protection, and how these duties are put into practice. Notably, the Commission should factor in the third country's ratification of the Council of Europe Convention of 28 January 1981 for the Protection of Individuals with regard to the Automatic Processing of Personal Data and its Additional Protocol. The Commission should seek the Board's advice when evaluating the standard of protection in third countries or international organisations.

text: The principle of transparency requires that any information addressed to the public or to the data subject be concise, easily accessible and easy to understand, and that clear and plain language and, additionally, where appropriate, visualisation be used. Such information could be provided in electronic form, for example, when addressed to the public, through a website. This is of particular relevance in situations where the proliferation of actors and the technological complexity of practice make it difficult for the data subject to know and understand whether, by whom and for what purpose personal data relating to him or her are being collected, such as in the case of online advertising. Given that children merit specific protection, any information and communication, where processing is addressed to a child, should be in such a clear and plain language that the child can easily understand.
rewrite: The principle of transparency demands that information directed at the public or data subjects be clear, accessible, and straightforward, using plain language and, where suitable, visual aids. This information may be delivered electronically, such as via a website for public communication.
