This is especially important in contexts where the number of involved parties and technical intricacies obscure how personal data is collected, by whom, and for what reasons, as seen with online advertising. Since children deserve particular safeguarding, any information and communication aimed at a child should be presented in exceptionally clear and simple terms for their comprehension.

text: This Regulation should apply to all matters concerning the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms vis-à- vis the processing of personal data which are not subject to specific obligations with the same objective set out in Directive 2002/58/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council (2), including the obligations on the controller and the rights of natural persons. In order to clarify the relationship between this Regulation and Directive 2002/58/EC, that Directive should be amended accordingly. Once this Regulation is adopted, Directive 2002/58/EC should be reviewed in particular in order to ensure consistency with this Regulation,
rewrite: This Regulation shall apply to all matters regarding the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms in relation to the processing of personal data not covered by specific obligations with equivalent aims under Directive 2002/58/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council (2), encompassing the duties of controllers and the rights of individuals. To clarify the relationship between this Regulation and Directive 2002/58/EC, that Directive should be amended as necessary. Following the adoption of this Regulation, Directive 2002/58/EC should be reassessed, particularly to ensure alignment with this Regulation.

text: The examination procedure should be used for the adoption of implementing acts on standard contractual clauses between controllers and processors and between processors; codes of conduct; technical standards and mechanisms for certification; the adequate level of protection afforded by a third country, a territory or a specified sector within that third country, or an international organisation; standard protection clauses; formats and procedures for the exchange of information by electronic means between controllers, processors and supervisory authorities for binding corporate rules; mutual assistance; and arrangements for the exchange of information by electronic means between supervisory authorities, and between supervisory authorities and the Board.
rewrite: The examination process should be applied for adopting implementing acts concerning standard contractual clauses for controllers and processors, as well as between processors; codes of conduct; technical standards and certification mechanisms; the adequacy of protection provided by a third country, territory, specified sector, or international organization; standard protection clauses; formats and procedures for electronic information exchange among controllers, processors, and supervisory authorities regarding binding corporate rules; mutual assistance; and arrangements for electronic information exchange between supervisory authorities, and between supervisory authorities and the Board.

text: Modalities should be provided for facilitating the exercise of the data subject's rights under this Regulation, including mechanisms to request and, if applicable, obtain, free of charge, in particular, access to and rectification or erasure of personal data and the exercise of the right to object. The controller should also provide means for requests to be made electronically, especially where personal data are processed by electronic means. The controller should be obliged to respond to requests from the data subject without undue delay and at the latest within one month and to give reasons where the controller does not intend to comply with any such requests.
rewrite: Mechanisms must be established to enable data subjects to exercise their rights under this Regulation effectively. These should include procedures for making requests and, where relevant, obtaining—free of charge—access to, rectification of, or erasure of personal data, as well as for objecting to processing. Controllers should also offer electronic channels for submitting requests, particularly when personal data are processed electronically. Controllers are required to respond to data subjects’ requests without undue delay and within one month at the latest, providing reasons if they decide not to comply.

text: Where the supervisory authority with which the complaint has been lodged is not the lead supervisory authority, the lead supervisory authority should closely cooperate with the supervisory authority with which the complaint has been lodged in accordance with the provisions on cooperation and consistency laid down in this Regulation. In such cases, the lead supervisory authority should, when taking measures intended to produce legal effects, including the imposition of administrative fines, take utmost account of the view of the supervisory authority with which the complaint has been lodged and which should remain competent to carry out any investigation on the territory of its own Member State in liaison with the competent supervisory authority.
rewrite: When the supervisory authority receiving the complaint is not the lead supervisory authority, the lead authority must cooperate closely with the receiving authority, following the cooperation and consistency rules set out in this Regulation. In such situations, the lead authority should give utmost consideration to the views of the receiving authority when adopting measures with legal effects, such as imposing administrative fines. The receiving authority should retain the competence to conduct any investigation within its own Member State, in coordination with the competent supervisory authority.

text: The legal systems of Denmark and Estonia do not allow for administrative fines as set out in this Regulation. The rules on administrative fines may be applied in such a manner that in Denmark the fine is imposed by competent national courts as a criminal penalty and in Estonia the fine is imposed by the supervisory authority in the framework of a misdemeanour procedure, provided that such an application of the rules in those Member States has an equivalent effect to administrative fines imposed by supervisory authorities. Therefore the competent national courts should take into account the recommendation by the supervisory authority initiating the fine. In any event, the fines imposed should be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.
rewrite: The legal frameworks of Denmark and Estonia do not permit administrative fines as defined in this Regulation. The provisions on administrative fines may be implemented so that in Denmark, the penalty is issued by relevant national courts as a criminal sanction, and in Estonia, it is levied by the supervisory authority within a misdemeanour process, as long as this application in those Member States achieves an effect equivalent to administrative fines imposed by supervisory authorities. Consequently, the competent national courts should consider the recommendation from the supervisory authority that initiates the fine. In all cases, the fines applied must be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive.

text: Guidance on the implementation of appropriate measures and on the demonstration of compliance by the controller or the processor, especially as regards the identification of the risk related to the processing, their assessment in terms of origin, nature, likelihood and severity, and the identification of best practices to mitigate the risk, could be provided in particular by means of approved codes of conduct, approved certifications, guidelines provided by the Board or indications provided by a data protection officer. The Board may also issue guidelines on processing operations that are considered to be unlikely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons and indicate what measures may be sufficient in such cases to address such risk.
rewrite: Guidance regarding the application of suitable measures and the demonstration of compliance by the controller or processor—particularly concerning the identification of processing-related risks, their evaluation in terms of source, nature, probability, and severity, and the determination of best practices to mitigate risk—may be furnished notably through approved codes of conduct, approved certifications, guidelines from the Board, or advice from a data protection officer. The Board may also provide guidelines on processing operations deemed unlikely to pose a high risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, and specify which measures could be adequate in such instances to manage that risk.

text: While this Regulation applies, inter alia, to the activities of courts and other judicial authorities, Union or Member State law could specify the processing operations and processing procedures in relation to the processing of personal data by courts and other judicial authorities. The competence of the supervisory authorities should not cover the processing of personal data when courts are acting in their judicial capacity, in order to safeguard the independence of the judiciary in the performance of its judicial tasks, including decision- making. It should be possible to entrust supervision of such data processing operations to specific bodies within the judicial system of the Member State, which should, in particular ensure compliance with the rules of this Regulation, enhance awareness among members of the judiciary of their obligations under this Regulation and handle complaints in relation to such data processing operations.
rewrite: Although this Regulation also governs the activities of courts and judicial authorities, Union or Member State law may define the specific processing operations and procedures for personal data handled by these entities. To preserve judicial independence in carrying out judicial functions, including decision-making, the supervisory authorities' jurisdiction should not extend to personal data processing when courts are acting judicially. Supervision of such data processing could be assigned to dedicated bodies within a Member State's judicial system. These bodies should notably ensure adherence to this Regulation's rules, promote judicial awareness of obligations under this Regulation, and address complaints concerning these data processing activities.

text: Member State law or collective agreements, including ‘works agreements’, may provide for specific rules on the processing of employees' personal data in the employment context, in particular for the conditions under which personal data in the employment context may be processed on the basis of the consent of the employee, the purposes of the recruitment, the performance of the contract of employment, including discharge of obligations laid down by law or by collective agreements, management, planning and organisation of work, equality and diversity in the workplace, health and safety at work, and for the purposes of the exercise and enjoyment, on an individual or collective basis, of rights and benefits related to employment, and for the purpose of the termination of the employment relationship.
rewrite: National legislation or collective bargaining arrangements, such as workplace agreements, can establish particular regulations governing the handling of employee personal data within employment settings. This includes stipulating the circumstances in which such data may be processed based on employee consent, as well as the purposes related to recruitment, fulfilling employment contract duties—including legal or collectively agreed obligations—work management, planning and organisation, promoting workplace equality and diversity, ensuring occupational health and safety, and enabling the exercise and receipt of individual or collective employment-related rights and benefits, along with managing the conclusion of the employment relationship.

text: Regulation (EC) No 45/2001 of the European Parliament and of the Council (2) applies to the processing of personal data by the Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies. Regulation (EC) No 45/2001 and other Union legal acts applicable to such processing of personal data should be adapted to the principles and rules established in this Regulation and applied in the light of this Regulation. In order to provide a strong and coherent data protection framework in the Union, the necessary adaptations of Regulation (EC) No 45/2001 should follow after the adoption of this Regulation, in order to allow application at the same time as this Regulation.
rewrite: Regulation (EC) No 45/2001 of the European Parliament and of the Council (2) governs the processing of personal data by Union institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies. Regulation (EC) No 45/2001 and other Union legal instruments relevant to such personal data processing must be aligned with the principles and rules set out in this Regulation and interpreted in accordance with it. To ensure a robust and consistent data protection framework across the Union, the required adjustments to Regulation (EC) No 45/2001 should be made following the adoption of this Regulation, enabling simultaneous application.

text: In order to maintain security and to prevent processing in infringement of this Regulation, the controller or processor should evaluate the risks inherent in the processing and implement measures to mitigate those risks, such as encryption. Those measures should ensure an appropriate level of security, including confidentiality, taking into account the state of the art and the costs of implementation in relation to the risks and the nature of the personal data to be protected. In assessing data security risk, consideration should be given to the risks that are presented by personal data processing, such as accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data transmitted, stored or otherwise processed which may in particular lead to physical, material or non-material damage.
rewrite: To uphold security and avoid processing that violates this Regulation, controllers or processors must assess the inherent risks in data handling and adopt measures like encryption to reduce them. These measures should provide a suitable security level, covering confidentiality, while considering current technology, implementation costs relative to risks, and the nature of the personal data involved. When evaluating data security risks, attention should be paid to threats from processing personal data, including accidental or illegal destruction, loss, alteration, or unauthorized disclosure or access to transmitted, stored, or processed data, which could result in physical, material, or non-material harm.

text: The principles of fair and transparent processing require that the data subject be informed of the existence of the processing operation and its purposes. The controller should provide the data subject with any further information necessary to ensure fair and transparent processing taking into account the specific circumstances and context in which the personal data are processed. Furthermore, the data subject should be informed of the existence of profiling and the consequences of such profiling. Where the personal data are collected from the data subject, the data subject should also be informed whether he or she is obliged to provide the personal data and of the consequences, where he or she does not provide such data. That information may be provided in combination with standardised icons in order to give in an easily visible, intelligible and clearly legible manner, a meaningful overview of the intended processing. Where the icons are presented electronically, they should be machine-readable.
rewrite: The principles of fair and transparent processing demand that data subjects be notified about the processing operation and its objectives. Controllers must supply any additional details needed to guarantee fairness and transparency, considering the particular conditions and context of the personal data processing. Additionally, data subjects should be made aware of any profiling activities and their potential effects. When personal data is obtained directly from the data subject, they must also be told if providing the data is mandatory and what the repercussions are for not supplying it. This information can be delivered alongside standardized icons to offer a clear, understandable, and easily readable summary of the planned processing. If the icons are displayed electronically, they should be machine-readable.

text: The responsibility and liability of the controller for any processing of personal data carried out by the controller or on the controller's behalf should be established. In particular, the controller should be obliged to implement appropriate and effective measures and be able to demonstrate the compliance of processing activities with this Regulation, including the effectiveness of the measures. Those measures should take into account the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing and the risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. 4.5.2016 EN Official Journal of the European Union L 119/15
rewrite: The controller's responsibility and liability for any personal data processing conducted by or on behalf of the controller must be clearly defined. Specifically, the controller should be required to adopt suitable and effective measures and to verify that processing activities comply with this Regulation, including the efficacy of these measures. Such measures must account for the processing's nature, scope, context, and purposes, as well as the risks to individuals' rights and freedoms. 4.5.2016 EN Official Journal of the European Union L 119/15

text: Public authorities to which personal data are disclosed in accordance with a legal obligation for the exercise of their official mission, such as tax and customs authorities, financial investigation units, independent adminis­ trative authorities, or financial market authorities responsible for the regulation and supervision of securities markets should not be regarded as recipients if they receive personal data which are necessary to carry out a particular inquiry in the general interest, in accordance with Union or Member State law. The requests for disclosure sent by the public authorities should always be in writing, reasoned and occasional and should not concern the entirety of a filing system or lead to the interconnection of filing systems. The processing of personal data by those public authorities should comply with the applicable data-protection rules according to the purposes of the processing.
rewrite: Public authorities that receive personal data under a legal obligation to fulfill their official duties—such as tax and customs agencies, financial investigation units, independent administrative bodies, or financial market regulators overseeing securities markets—should not be considered recipients when they obtain data required for a specific inquiry serving the public interest, as per Union or Member State law. Disclosure requests from these authorities must always be written, justified, and infrequent, and should not target entire filing systems or enable the linking of such systems. The processing of personal data by these public authorities must adhere to applicable data-protection regulations, consistent with the processing purposes.

text: The controller should communicate to the data subject a personal data breach, without undue delay, where that personal data breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of the natural person in order to allow him or her to take the necessary precautions. The communication should describe the nature of the personal data breach as well as recommendations for the natural person concerned to mitigate potential adverse effects. Such communications to data subjects should be made as soon as reasonably feasible and in close cooperation with the supervisory authority, respecting guidance provided by it or by other relevant authorities such as law-enforcement authorities. For example, the need to mitigate an immediate risk of damage would call for prompt communication with data subjects whereas the need to implement appropriate measures against continuing or similar personal data breaches may justify more time for communication.
rewrite: The controller must inform the data subject of a personal data breach without undue delay when the breach is likely to pose a high risk to the individual's rights and freedoms, enabling them to take necessary precautions. This notification should outline the breach's nature and include recommendations for the affected person to lessen possible negative impacts. These communications to data subjects should occur as soon as reasonably practicable, in close coordination with the supervisory authority, and in accordance with guidance from it or other relevant bodies like law enforcement. For instance, an immediate risk of harm necessitates swift notification, while the need to establish suitable measures for ongoing or similar breaches may allow more time for communication.

text: The Commission may recognise that a third country, a territory or a specified sector within a third country, or an international organisation no longer ensures an adequate level of data protection. Consequently the transfer of personal data to that third country or international organisation should be prohibited, unless the requirements in this Regulation relating to transfers subject to appropriate safeguards, including binding corporate rules, and derogations for specific situations are fulfilled. In that case, provision should be made for consultations between the Commission and such third countries or international organisations. The Commission should, in a timely manner, inform the third country or international organisation of the reasons and enter into consultations with it in order to remedy the situation.
rewrite: The Commission may determine that a third country, territory, specified sector within a third country, or an international organization no longer provides an adequate level of data protection. As a result, transfers of personal data to that third country or international organization shall be prohibited, unless the requirements under this Regulation for transfers subject to appropriate safeguards—such as binding corporate rules—and derogations for particular situations are met. In such instances, arrangements should be established for consultations between the Commission and the relevant third countries or international organizations. The Commission should promptly notify the third country or international organization of the reasons and engage in consultations to resolve the matter.

text: The processing of personal data should be designed to serve mankind. The right to the protection of personal data is not an absolute right; it must be considered in relation to its function in society and be balanced against other fundamental rights, in accordance with the principle of proportionality. This Regulation respects all fundamental rights and observes the freedoms and principles recognised in the Charter as enshrined in the Treaties, in particular the respect for private and family life, home and communications, the protection of personal data, freedom of thought, conscience and religion, freedom of expression and information, freedom to conduct a business, the right to an effective remedy and to a fair trial, and cultural, religious and linguistic diversity.
rewrite: The handling of personal data ought to be structured to benefit humanity. The entitlement to personal data protection is not an absolute right; it should be evaluated in light of its societal role and weighed against other fundamental rights, following the principle of proportionality. This Regulation upholds all fundamental rights and adheres to the freedoms and principles affirmed in the Charter as established by the Treaties, including respect for private and family life, home and correspondence, the safeguarding of personal data, freedom of thought, conscience, and religion, freedom of expression and information, the freedom to engage in business, the right to an effective remedy and a fair trial, as well as cultural, religious, and linguistic diversity.

text: By coupling information from registries, researchers can obtain new knowledge of great value with regard to widespread medical conditions such as cardiovascular disease, cancer and depression. On the basis of registries, research results can be enhanced, as they draw on a larger population. Within social science, research on the basis of registries enables researchers to obtain essential knowledge about the long-term correlation of a number of social conditions such as unemployment and education with other life conditions. Research results obtained through registries provide solid, high-quality knowledge which can provide the basis for the formulation and implementation of knowledge-based policy, improve the quality of life for a number of people and improve the efficiency of social services. In order to facilitate scientific research, personal data can be processed for scientific research purposes, subject to appropriate conditions and safeguards set out in Union or Member State law.
rewrite: By linking data from registries, researchers can gain valuable new insights into widespread health issues like cardiovascular disease, cancer, and depression. Registry-based research strengthens findings by utilizing larger populations. In social science, such research allows experts to uncover key long-term relationships between various social factors—such as unemployment and education—and other life circumstances. Findings derived from registries offer robust, high-quality evidence that can inform the creation and execution of evidence-based policies, enhance quality of life for many, and boost the efficiency of social services. To support scientific inquiry, personal data may be processed for research purposes under suitable conditions and safeguards established in Union or Member State legislation.

text: Each supervisory authority should be competent on the territory of its own Member State to exercise the powers and to perform the tasks conferred on it in accordance with this Regulation. This should cover in particular the 4.5.2016 EN Official Journal of the European Union L 119/23 processing in the context of the activities of an establishment of the controller or processor on the territory of its own Member State, the processing of personal data carried out by public authorities or private bodies acting in the public interest, processing affecting data subjects on its territory or processing carried out by a controller or processor not established in the Union when targeting data subjects residing on its territory. This should include handling complaints lodged by a data subject, conducting investigations on the application of this Regulation and promoting public awareness of the risks, rules, safeguards and rights in relation to the processing of personal data.
rewrite: Each supervisory authority must have jurisdiction within its own Member State to implement the powers and duties assigned by this Regulation. This specifically includes 4.5.2016 EN Official Journal of the European Union L 119/23 processing within activities of a controller’s or processor’s establishment in its own Member State, processing by public authorities or private entities serving the public interest, processing impacting data subjects on its territory, or processing by controllers or processors outside the Union that targets residents on its territory. It should also involve addressing complaints from data subjects, investigating compliance with this Regulation, and raising public awareness about risks, regulations, protections, and rights concerning personal data processing.

text: Since the objective of this Regulation, namely to ensure an equivalent level of protection of natural persons and the free flow of personal data throughout the Union, cannot be sufficiently achieved by the Member States and can rather, by reason of the scale or effects of the action, be better achieved at Union level, the Union may adopt measures, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity as set out in Article 5 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU). In accordance with the principle of proportionality as set out in that Article, this Regulation does not go beyond what is necessary in order to achieve that objective.
rewrite: Given that the aim of this Regulation—to secure a uniform level of protection for individuals and the unimpeded movement of personal data across the Union—cannot be adequately attained by Member States individually and is more effectively realized at Union level due to the scope or impact of such measures, the Union may enact actions following the subsidiarity principle outlined in Article 5 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU). Consistent with the proportionality principle in the same Article, this Regulation remains confined to what is essential for fulfilling that objective.

text: The objectives and principles of Directive 95/46/EC remain sound, but it has not prevented fragmentation in the implementation of data protection across the Union, legal uncertainty or a widespread public perception that there are significant risks to the protection of natural persons, in particular with regard to online activity. Differences in the level of protection of the rights and freedoms of natural persons, in particular the right to the protection of personal data, with regard to the processing of personal data in the Member States may prevent the free flow of personal data throughout the Union. Those differences may therefore constitute an obstacle to the pursuit of economic activities at the level of the Union, distort competition and impede authorities in the discharge of their responsibilities under Union law. Such a difference in levels of protection is due to the existence of differences in the implementation and application of Directive 95/46/EC.
rewrite: The goals and principles of Directive 95/46/EC are still valid, yet it has failed to stop fragmentation in how data protection is applied across the Union, legal ambiguity, or a common public view that substantial risks exist to safeguarding individuals, especially concerning online actions. Variances in safeguarding the rights and freedoms of individuals, notably the right to personal data protection, regarding personal data processing in Member States can hinder the free movement of such data within the Union. These disparities may thus create a barrier to conducting economic activities at the Union level, distort competition, and hinder authorities in fulfilling their duties under Union law. This divergence in protection levels stems from differences in how Directive 95/46/EC is implemented and enforced.

text: In applying the consistency mechanism, the Board should, within a determined period of time, issue an opinion, if a majority of its members so decides or if so requested by any supervisory authority concerned or the Commission. The Board should also be empowered to adopt legally binding decisions where there are disputes between supervisory authorities. For that purpose, it should issue, in principle by a two-thirds majority of its members, legally binding decisions in clearly specified cases where there are conflicting views among supervisory authorities, in particular in the cooperation mechanism between the lead supervisory authority and supervisory authorities concerned on the merits of the case, in particular whether there is an infringement of this Regulation.
rewrite: When employing the consistency mechanism, the Board must issue an opinion within a set timeframe, if a majority of its members decides to do so or if requested by any concerned supervisory authority or the Commission. The Board should also have the authority to make legally binding decisions in cases of disputes between supervisory authorities. To this end, it should adopt, typically by a two-thirds majority of its members, legally binding decisions in clearly defined situations involving conflicting views among supervisory authorities. This applies especially within the cooperation framework between the lead supervisory authority and the concerned supervisory authorities regarding the case's substance, particularly in determining whether there has been a breach of this Regulation.

text: Where personal data are processed for archiving purposes, this Regulation should also apply to that processing, bearing in mind that this Regulation should not apply to deceased persons. Public authorities or public or private bodies that hold records of public interest should be services which, pursuant to Union or Member State law, have a legal obligation to acquire, preserve, appraise, arrange, describe, communicate, promote, disseminate and provide access to records of enduring value for general public interest. Member States should also be authorised to provide for the further processing of personal data for archiving purposes, for example with a view to providing specific information related to the political behaviour under former totalitarian state regimes, genocide, crimes against humanity, in particular the Holocaust, or war crimes. L 119/30 EN Official Journal of the European Union 4.5.2016
rewrite: When personal data is handled for archival purposes, this Regulation should continue to apply, while noting that it does not cover deceased individuals. Public authorities or other entities, whether public or private, that maintain records of public interest should be those services that, under Union or Member State legislation, are legally required to obtain, keep, evaluate, organize, describe, share, promote, distribute, and allow access to records of lasting value for the broader public interest. Member States should also be permitted to allow additional processing of personal data for archival reasons, such as to furnish particular information concerning political conduct under past totalitarian governments, acts of genocide, crimes against humanity, especially the Holocaust, or war crimes. L 119/30 EN Official Journal of the European Union 4.5.2016

text: Where personal data are processed for statistical purposes, this Regulation should apply to that processing. Union or Member State law should, within the limits of this Regulation, determine statistical content, control of access, specifications for the processing of personal data for statistical purposes and appropriate measures to safeguard the rights and freedoms of the data subject and for ensuring statistical confidentiality. Statistical purposes mean any operation of collection and the processing of personal data necessary for statistical surveys or for the production of statistical results. Those statistical results may further be used for different purposes, including a scientific research purpose. The statistical purpose implies that the result of processing for statistical purposes is not personal data, but aggregate data, and that this result or the personal data are not used in support of measures or decisions regarding any particular natural person.
rewrite: When personal data is processed for statistical purposes, this Regulation governs such processing. Union or Member State law should, within the scope of this Regulation, define statistical content, regulate access, set specifications for processing personal data for statistical purposes, and establish suitable safeguards for the rights and freedoms of data subjects, as well as ensure statistical confidentiality. Statistical purposes refer to any collection and processing of personal data required for statistical surveys or to generate statistical results. These statistical results may subsequently be applied for various objectives, including scientific research. The statistical purpose indicates that the outcome of processing for such purposes is not personal data but aggregated data, and that neither this result nor the personal data are employed to inform measures or decisions concerning any specific individual.

text: The general conditions for the member or members of the supervisory authority should be laid down by law in each Member State and should in particular provide that those members are to be appointed, by means of a transparent procedure, either by the parliament, government or the head of State of the Member State on the basis of a proposal from the government, a member of the government, the parliament or a chamber of the parliament, or by an independent body entrusted under Member State law. In order to ensure the independence of the supervisory authority, the member or members should act with integrity, refrain from any action that is incompatible with their duties and should not, during their term of office, engage in any incompatible occupation, whether gainful or not. The supervisory authority should have its own staff, chosen by the supervisory authority or an independent body established by Member State law, which should be subject to the exclusive direction of the member or members of the supervisory authority.
rewrite: The general requirements for supervisory authority members must be established by law in each Member State. These laws should specify that members are appointed through a transparent process, either by the parliament, government, or head of state based on a proposal from the government, a government member, the parliament, or a parliamentary chamber, or by an independent body designated under national law. To safeguard the authority's independence, members must act with integrity, avoid any conduct inconsistent with their responsibilities, and not pursue any conflicting activities, paid or unpaid, during their tenure. The supervisory authority should employ its own personnel, selected either by the authority itself or by an independent body created by national law, who must work solely under the direction of the authority's members.

text: Where a data protection impact assessment indicates that the processing would, in the absence of safeguards, security measures and mechanisms to mitigate the risk, result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons and the controller is of the opinion that the risk cannot be mitigated by reasonable means in terms of available technologies and costs of implementation, the supervisory authority should be consulted prior to the start of processing activities. Such high risk is likely to result from certain types of processing and the extent and frequency of processing, which may result also in a realisation of damage or interference with the rights and freedoms of the natural person. The supervisory authority should respond to the request for consultation within a specified period. However, the absence of a reaction of the supervisory authority within that period should be without prejudice to any intervention of the supervisory authority in accordance with its tasks and powers laid down in this Regulation, including the power to prohibit processing operations. As part of that consultation process, the outcome of a data protection impact assessment carried out with regard to the processing at issue may be submitted to the supervisory authority, in particular the measures envisaged to mitigate the risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.
rewrite: When a data protection impact assessment shows that processing would pose a high risk to individuals' rights and freedoms without adequate safeguards, security measures, or risk mitigation, and the controller believes the risk cannot be reasonably addressed considering available technology and implementation costs, the supervisory authority must be consulted before processing begins. Such high risk may arise from specific processing types, scale, and frequency, potentially leading to harm or infringement of individual rights. The supervisory authority should reply within a set timeframe. Still, its lack of response within that period does not affect its ability to intervene under this Regulation's tasks and powers, such as banning processing activities. During consultation, the results of the relevant data protection impact assessment may be provided to the supervisory authority, especially the planned steps to reduce risks to individuals' rights and freedoms.

text: Where processing is based on the data subject's consent, the controller should be able to demonstrate that the data subject has given consent to the processing operation. In particular in the context of a written declaration on another matter, safeguards should ensure that the data subject is aware of the fact that and the extent to which consent is given. In accordance with Council Directive 93/13/EEC (1) a declaration of consent pre- formulated by the controller should be provided in an intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language and it should not contain unfair terms. For consent to be informed, the data subject should be aware at least of the identity of the controller and the purposes of the processing for which the personal data are intended. Consent should not be regarded as freely given if the data subject has no genuine or free choice or is unable to refuse or withdraw consent without detriment.
rewrite: When processing relies on the data subject's consent, the controller must be capable of proving that consent was granted for the processing activity. Especially within a written statement concerning a different issue, protective measures must guarantee the data subject understands both that consent is being provided and its specific scope. In line with Council Directive 93/13/EEC (1), any pre-drafted consent statement from the controller should be presented in a clear, accessible format, using straightforward language and avoiding unfair conditions. To ensure consent is informed, the data subject must at minimum know the controller's identity and the intended purposes for processing the personal data. Consent cannot be considered freely given if the data subject lacks a real or free choice, or if refusing or retracting consent results in negative consequences.

text: In order to strengthen the enforcement of the rules of this Regulation, penalties including administrative fines should be imposed for any infringement of this Regulation, in addition to, or instead of appropriate measures imposed by the supervisory authority pursuant to this Regulation. In a case of a minor infringement or if the fine likely to be imposed would constitute a disproportionate burden to a natural person, a reprimand may be issued instead of a fine. Due regard should however be given to the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement, the intentional character of the infringement, actions taken to mitigate the damage suffered, degree of responsibility or any relevant previous infringements, the manner in which the infringement became known to the supervisory authority, compliance with measures ordered against the controller or processor, adherence to a code of conduct and any other aggravating or mitigating factor. The imposition of penalties including administrative fines should be subject to appropriate procedural safeguards in accordance with the general principles of Union law and the Charter, including effective judicial protection and due process.
rewrite: To ensure robust enforcement of this Regulation's provisions, administrative fines should be applied for any violation, either in addition to or in place of other corrective measures ordered by the supervisory authority. For minor infringements or where a fine would impose a disproportionate hardship on an individual, a reprimand may be substituted. Consideration must be given to the infringement's nature, severity, and duration, its intentional character, steps taken to mitigate harm, the degree of responsibility, any prior infringements, how the breach was discovered, adherence to prior orders, compliance with codes of conduct, and other aggravating or mitigating circumstances. The application of such penalties, including fines, must adhere to proper procedural safeguards under Union law and the Charter, ensuring effective judicial remedy and due process.

text: Consent should be given by a clear affirmative act establishing a freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of the data subject's agreement to the processing of personal data relating to him or her, such as by a written statement, including by electronic means, or an oral statement. This could include ticking a box when visiting an internet website, choosing technical settings for information society services or another statement or conduct which clearly indicates in this context the data subject's acceptance of the proposed processing of his or her personal data. Silence, pre-ticked boxes or inactivity should not therefore constitute consent. Consent should cover all processing activities carried out for the same purpose or purposes. When the processing has multiple purposes, consent should be given for all of them. If the data subject's consent is to be given following a request by electronic means, the request must be clear, concise and not unnecessarily disruptive to the use of the service for which it is provided.
rewrite: Consent must be expressed through a clear, affirmative action that demonstrates a freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous agreement by the data subject to the processing of their personal data. This may be done via a written or oral statement, including through electronic means. Examples include ticking a box on a website, selecting technical settings for online services, or any other statement or behavior that unambiguously signifies acceptance of the proposed data processing. Silence, pre-checked boxes, or inaction should not be considered valid consent. Consent should apply to all processing activities undertaken for the same purpose or purposes. Where processing serves multiple purposes, consent must be obtained for each. If consent is requested electronically, the request should be clear, succinct, and not unduly interfere with the use of the service in question.

text: Provisions should be made for the possibility for transfers in certain circumstances where the data subject has given his or her explicit consent, where the transfer is occasional and necessary in relation to a contract or a legal claim, regardless of whether in a judicial procedure or whether in an administrative or any out-of-court procedure, including procedures before regulatory bodies. Provision should also be made for the possibility for transfers where important grounds of public interest laid down by Union or Member State law so require or where the transfer is made from a register established by law and intended for consultation by the public or persons having a legitimate interest. In the latter case, such a transfer should not involve the entirety of the personal data or entire categories of the data contained in the register and, when the register is intended for consultation by persons having a legitimate interest, the transfer should be made only at the request of those persons or, if they are to be the recipients, taking into full account the interests and fundamental rights of the data subject.
rewrite: Arrangements must allow for transfers under specific conditions, such as when the data subject has provided explicit consent, or when the transfer is occasional and required for a contract or legal claim, whether in judicial, administrative, or out-of-court proceedings, including those before regulatory bodies. Provisions should also permit transfers when essential public interest grounds under Union or Member State law necessitate it, or when the transfer originates from a legally established register meant for public access or for individuals with a legitimate interest. In this last scenario, the transfer must not cover all personal data or entire data categories in the register. If the register is for consultation by those with a legitimate interest, transfers should occur only upon their request or, if they are the recipients, with full consideration of the data subject's interests and fundamental rights.

text: A personal data breach may, if not addressed in an appropriate and timely manner, result in physical, material or non-material damage to natural persons such as loss of control over their personal data or limitation of their rights, discrimination, identity theft or fraud, financial loss, unauthorised reversal of pseudonymisation, damage to reputation, loss of confidentiality of personal data protected by professional secrecy or any other significant economic or social disadvantage to the natural person concerned. Therefore, as soon as the controller becomes 4.5.2016 EN Official Journal of the European Union L 119/17 aware that a personal data breach has occurred, the controller should notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, unless the controller is able to demonstrate, in accordance with the accountability principle, that the personal data breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. Where such notification cannot be achieved within 72 hours, the reasons for the delay should accompany the notification and information may be provided in phases without undue further delay.
rewrite: A personal data breach, if not properly and promptly addressed, can lead to physical, material, or non-material harm to individuals. This includes loss of control over personal data, restriction of rights, discrimination, identity theft, fraud, financial loss, unauthorized reversal of pseudonymization, reputational damage, breach of confidentiality under professional secrecy, or other significant economic or social harm. Consequently, once the controller becomes aware of a personal data breach, they must report it to the supervisory authority without undue delay, ideally within 72 hours of awareness, unless the controller can show, under the accountability principle, that the breach is unlikely to pose a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms. If notification within 72 hours is not possible, the reasons for the delay must be included with the report, and information may be submitted in stages without further undue delay.

text: Where personal data are processed for scientific research purposes, this Regulation should also apply to that processing. For the purposes of this Regulation, the processing of personal data for scientific research purposes should be interpreted in a broad manner including for example technological development and demonstration, fundamental research, applied research and privately funded research. In addition, it should take into account the Union's objective under Article 179(1) TFEU of achieving a European Research Area. Scientific research purposes should also include studies conducted in the public interest in the area of public health. To meet the specificities of processing personal data for scientific research purposes, specific conditions should apply in particular as regards the publication or otherwise disclosure of personal data in the context of scientific research purposes. If the result of scientific research in particular in the health context gives reason for further measures in the interest of the data subject, the general rules of this Regulation should apply in view of those measures.
rewrite: When personal data is handled for scientific research, this Regulation should govern such processing. For the purposes of this Regulation, scientific research should be understood broadly, encompassing areas like technological development and demonstration, basic research, applied research, and privately funded research. It should also consider the Union’s goal, under Article 179(1) TFEU, of establishing a European Research Area. Scientific research purposes should further cover studies carried out in the public interest within public health. To address the unique aspects of processing personal data for scientific research, particular conditions should be set, especially regarding the publication or other disclosure of such data for research aims. If scientific research outcomes, particularly in health, justify additional measures for the data subject’s benefit, the general provisions of this Regulation should apply to those measures.

text: This Regulation allows the principle of public access to official documents to be taken into account when applying this Regulation. Public access to official documents may be considered to be in the public interest. Personal data in documents held by a public authority or a public body should be able to be publicly disclosed by that authority or body if the disclosure is provided for by Union or Member State law to which the public authority or public body is subject. Such laws should reconcile public access to official documents and the reuse of public sector information with the right to the protection of personal data and may therefore provide for the necessary reconciliation with the right to the protection of personal data pursuant to this Regulation. The reference to public authorities and bodies should in that context include all authorities or other bodies covered by Member State law on public access to documents. Directive 2003/98/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council (1) leaves intact and in no way affects the level of protection of natural persons with regard to the
rewrite: This Regulation permits the principle of public access to official documents to be considered in its application. Public access to such documents may be deemed to serve the public interest. Personal data contained in documents held by a public authority or body may be disclosed by that entity if disclosure is mandated by Union or Member State law applicable to it. These laws should balance public access to official documents and the reuse of public sector information with the right to personal data protection, and may thus establish the necessary alignment with data protection rights under this Regulation. In this context, references to public authorities and bodies should encompass all entities subject to Member State laws on public document access. text: Transfers which can be qualified as not repetitive and that only concern a limited number of data subjects, could also be possible for the purposes of the compelling legitimate interests pursued by the controller, when those interests are not overridden by the interests or rights and freedoms of the data subject and when the controller has assessed all the circumstances surrounding the data transfer. The controller should give particular considera­ tion to the nature of the personal data, the purpose and duration of the proposed processing operation or operations, as well as the situation in the country of origin, the third country and the country of final destination, and should provide suitable safeguards to protect fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons with regard to the processing of their personal data. Such transfers should be possible only in residual cases where none of the other grounds for transfer are applicable. For scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes, the legitimate expectations of society for an increase of knowledge should be taken into con­ sideration. The controller should inform the supervisory authority and the data subject about the transfer.
rewrite: Transfers that are non-repetitive and involve only a limited number of individuals may also be permissible when driven by the controller's compelling legitimate interests, provided these interests do not outweigh the rights and freedoms of the data subjects and after a thorough assessment of all transfer circumstances. The controller must carefully evaluate the type of personal data, the purpose and length of the intended processing, as well as conditions in the source, third, and destination countries, and must implement appropriate safeguards to uphold individuals' fundamental rights regarding their data processing. Such transfers should be allowed only in exceptional cases where no other transfer grounds apply. For scientific, historical research, or statistical aims, societal expectations for advancing knowledge should be considered. The controller is required to notify both the supervisory authority and the data subject about the transfer.

text: The information in relation to the processing of personal data relating to the data subject should be given to him or her at the time of collection from the data subject, or, where the personal data are obtained from another source, within a reasonable period, depending on the circumstances of the case. Where personal data can be legitimately disclosed to another recipient, the data subject should be informed when the personal data are first disclosed to the recipient. Where the controller intends to process the personal data for a purpose other than that for which they were collected, the controller should provide the data subject prior to that further processing with information on that other purpose and other necessary information. Where the origin of the personal data cannot be provided to the data subject because various sources have been used, general information should be provided.
rewrite: Information regarding the processing of personal data concerning the data subject should be provided at the moment it is collected from them, or, if the data is acquired from a different source, within a suitable timeframe based on the specific situation. If personal data is lawfully shared with another recipient, the data subject must be notified upon the initial disclosure to that recipient. Should the controller plan to use the personal data for a purpose different from the original collection intent, they must inform the data subject beforehand about this new purpose and any other relevant details. In cases where the origin of the personal data cannot be specified due to the use of multiple sources, general information should be supplied.

text: The principles of data protection should apply to any information concerning an identified or identifiable natural person. Personal data which have undergone pseudonymisation, which could be attributed to a natural person by the use of additional information should be considered to be information on an identifiable natural person. To determine whether a natural person is identifiable, account should be taken of all the means reasonably likely to be used, such as singling out, either by the controller or by another person to identify the natural person directly or indirectly. To ascertain whether means are reasonably likely to be used to identify the natural person, account should be taken of all objective factors, such as the costs of and the amount of time required for identification, taking into consideration the available technology at the time of the processing and technological developments. The principles of data protection should therefore not apply to anonymous information, namely information which does not relate to an identified or identifiable natural person or to personal data rendered anonymous in such a manner that the data subject is not or no longer identifiable. This Regulation does not therefore concern the processing of such anonymous information, including for statistical or research purposes.
rewrite: Data protection principles must apply to all information related to an identified or identifiable individual. Pseudonymised personal data that can be linked to a person through additional details should be treated as information about an identifiable individual. To assess identifiability, all reasonably feasible methods should be considered, including those enabling singling out, whether used by the controller or others to identify someone directly or indirectly. In evaluating whether such methods are reasonably feasible, objective factors like the cost and time needed for identification must be weighed, accounting for current technology and its evolution. Consequently, data protection principles do not extend to anonymous information—that is, data not connected to an identified or identifiable person, or personal data anonymised so the individual cannot be identified. This Regulation thus does not govern the processing of such anonymous information, even for statistical or research purposes.

text: Where a court seized of proceedings against a decision by a supervisory authority has reason to believe that proceedings concerning the same processing, such as the same subject matter as regards processing by the same controller or processor, or the same cause of action, are brought before a competent court in another Member State, it should contact that court in order to confirm the existence of such related proceedings. If related proceedings are pending before a court in another Member State, any court other than the court first 4.5.2016 EN Official Journal of the European Union L 119/27 seized may stay its proceedings or may, on request of one of the parties, decline jurisdiction in favour of the court first seized if that court has jurisdiction over the proceedings in question and its law permits the consoli­ dation of such related proceedings. Proceedings are deemed to be related where they are so closely connected that it is expedient to hear and determine them together in order to avoid the risk of irreconcilable judgments resulting from separate proceedings.
rewrite: When a court handling a case against a decision by a supervisory authority has grounds to suspect that similar proceedings regarding the same processing activity—such as the same subject matter involving the same controller or processor, or the same legal claim—are initiated before a competent court in another Member State, it should contact that court to verify the existence of such related proceedings. If related proceedings are pending before a court in another Member State, any court other than the one first seized may suspend its proceedings or, upon request by a party, may decline jurisdiction in favor of the court first seized, provided that court has jurisdiction over the matters and its legal system allows for the consolidation of such related cases. Proceedings are considered related when they are so closely linked that it is advisable to hear and decide them jointly to prevent the risk of conflicting judgments arising from separate proceedings.

text: Where the processing is carried out by a public authority, except for courts or independent judicial authorities when acting in their judicial capacity, where, in the private sector, processing is carried out by a controller whose core activities consist of processing operations that require regular and systematic monitoring of the data subjects on a large scale, or where the core activities of the controller or the processor consist of processing on a large scale of special categories of personal data and data relating to criminal convictions and offences, a person with expert knowledge of data protection law and practices should assist the controller or processor to monitor internal compliance with this Regulation. In the private sector, the core activities of a controller relate to its primary activities and do not relate to the processing of personal data as ancillary activities. The necessary level of expert knowledge should be determined in particular according to the data processing operations carried out 4.5.2016 EN Official Journal of the European Union L 119/19 and the protection required for the personal data processed by the controller or the processor. Such data protection officers, whether or not they are an employee of the controller, should be in a position to perform their duties and tasks in an independent manner.
rewrite: When processing is conducted by a public authority—excluding courts or independent judicial bodies acting in a judicial capacity—or in the private sector by a controller whose principal activities involve large-scale, regular, and systematic monitoring of data subjects, or whose main operations consist of large-scale processing of special categories of personal data or data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, a data protection expert should support the controller or processor in overseeing internal adherence to this Regulation. In the private sector, a controller’s core activities refer to its primary business functions, not to ancillary personal data processing. The required expertise should be assessed based on the data processing conducted and the level of protection needed for the personal data handled by the controller or processor. These data protection officers, regardless of their employment status with the controller, must be able to carry out their duties independently.

text: Where a data subject considers that his or her rights under this Regulation are infringed, he or she should have the right to mandate a not-for-profit body, organisation or association which is constituted in accordance with the law of a Member State, has statutory objectives which are in the public interest and is active in the field of the protection of personal data to lodge a complaint on his or her behalf with a supervisory authority, exercise the right to a judicial remedy on behalf of data subjects or, if provided for in Member State law, exercise the right to receive compensation on behalf of data subjects. A Member State may provide for such a body, organisation or association to have the right to lodge a complaint in that Member State, independently of a data subject's mandate, and the right to an effective judicial remedy where it has reasons to consider that the rights of a data subject have been infringed as a result of the processing of personal data which infringes this Regulation. That body, organisation or association may not be allowed to claim compensation on a data subject's behalf indepen­ dently of the data subject's mandate.
rewrite: If a data subject believes their rights under this Regulation have been violated, they should be entitled to authorize a not-for-profit body, organization, or association that is legally established in a Member State, pursues public interest objectives, and is active in personal data protection to file a complaint on their behalf with a supervisory authority, pursue judicial remedies for data subjects, or, where permitted by Member State law, seek compensation on their behalf. A Member State may grant such an entity the right to lodge a complaint within its jurisdiction without a data subject’s specific mandate, and to seek effective judicial redress if it has grounds to believe a data subject’s rights have been breached due to processing that violates this Regulation. However, such an entity may not independently claim compensation on a data subject’s behalf without their authorization.

text: The protection of the rights and freedoms of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data require that appropriate technical and organisational measures be taken to ensure that the requirements of this Regulation are met. In order to be able to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation, the controller should adopt internal policies and implement measures which meet in particular the principles of data protection by design and data protection by default. Such measures could consist, inter alia, of minimising the processing of personal data, pseudonymising personal data as soon as possible, transparency with regard to the functions and processing of personal data, enabling the data subject to monitor the data processing, enabling the controller to create and improve security features. When developing, designing, selecting and using applications, services and products that are based on the processing of personal data or process personal data to fulfil their task, producers of the products, services and applications should be encouraged to take into account the right to data protection when developing and designing such products, services and applications and, with due regard to the state of the art, to make sure that controllers and processors are able to fulfil their data protection obligations. The principles of data protection by design and by default should also be taken into consideration in the context of public tenders.
rewrite: Safeguarding the rights and freedoms of individuals concerning personal data processing necessitates implementing suitable technical and organizational measures to fulfill this Regulation's requirements. To demonstrate compliance, controllers must establish internal policies and adopt measures that align with data protection by design and by default principles. These measures may include minimizing personal data processing, promptly pseudonymizing data, ensuring transparency about data functions and processing, allowing data subjects to oversee processing, and enabling controllers to enhance security features. When creating, designing, selecting, or utilizing applications, services, and products involving personal data processing, producers should be urged to consider data protection rights during development and design. They must also ensure, considering current technology, that controllers and processors can meet their data protection duties. Data protection by design and by default principles should further be integrated into public tender processes.

text: When personal data moves across borders outside the Union it may put at increased risk the ability of natural persons to exercise data protection rights in particular to protect themselves from the unlawful use or disclosure of that information. At the same time, supervisory authorities may find that they are unable to pursue complaints or conduct investigations relating to the activities outside their borders. Their efforts to work together in the cross-border context may also be hampered by insufficient preventative or remedial powers, inconsistent legal regimes, and practical obstacles like resource constraints. Therefore, there is a need to promote closer cooperation among data protection supervisory authorities to help them exchange information and carry out investigations with their international counterparts. For the purposes of developing international cooperation mechanisms to facilitate and provide international mutual assistance for the enforcement of legislation for the protection of personal data, the Commission and the supervisory authorities should exchange information and cooperate in activities related to the exercise of their powers with competent authorities in third countries, based on reciprocity and in accordance with this Regulation.
rewrite: When personal data is transferred beyond the Union's borders, it can heighten the risk that individuals may face difficulties in exercising their data protection rights, especially in safeguarding against the misuse or unauthorized disclosure of their information. Concurrently, supervisory authorities might encounter challenges in addressing complaints or conducting investigations into activities occurring outside their jurisdiction. Their collaborative efforts in cross-border situations can be further hindered by limited preventive or corrective powers, divergent legal frameworks, and practical barriers such as resource limitations. Consequently, fostering enhanced cooperation among data protection supervisory authorities is essential to support the sharing of information and the execution of investigations with international partners. To establish international cooperation mechanisms that aid in providing mutual assistance for enforcing personal data protection laws, the Commission and supervisory authorities should, on the basis of reciprocity and in line with this Regulation, engage in information exchange and collaborate with competent authorities in third countries on matters involving the use of their powers.

text: Personal data concerning health should include all data pertaining to the health status of a data subject which reveal information relating to the past, current or future physical or mental health status of the data subject. This includes information about the natural person collected in the course of the registration for, or the provision of, health care services as referred to in Directive 2011/24/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council (1) to that natural person; a number, symbol or particular assigned to a natural person to uniquely identify the natural person for health purposes; information derived from the testing or examination of a body part or bodily substance, including from genetic data and biological samples; and any information on, for example, a disease, disability, disease risk, medical history, clinical treatment or the physiological or biomedical state of the data subject independent of its source, for example from a physician or other health professional, a hospital, a medical device or an in vitro diagnostic test.
rewrite: Personal data related to health encompasses all information regarding an individual's health status that discloses details about their past, present, or future physical or mental condition. This comprises data gathered during the enrollment for or delivery of healthcare services as defined in Directive 2011/24/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council (1) to that individual; a unique identifier, such as a number, symbol, or code, assigned for health-related purposes; results from the analysis or testing of any body part or biological material, including genetic information and samples; and any details concerning, for instance, an illness, impairment, health risk, medical background, clinical care, or the physiological or biomedical condition of the individual, regardless of its origin—be it from a doctor, another healthcare provider, a hospital, a medical apparatus, or an in vitro diagnostic assessment.

text: Every data subject should have the right to lodge a complaint with a single supervisory authority, in particular in the Member State of his or her habitual residence, and the right to an effective judicial remedy in accordance L 119/26 EN Official Journal of the European Union 4.5.2016 with Article 47 of the Charter if the data subject considers that his or her rights under this Regulation are infringed or where the supervisory authority does not act on a complaint, partially or wholly rejects or dismisses a complaint or does not act where such action is necessary to protect the rights of the data subject. The investi­ gation following a complaint should be carried out, subject to judicial review, to the extent that is appropriate in the specific case. The supervisory authority should inform the data subject of the progress and the outcome of the complaint within a reasonable period. If the case requires further investigation or coordination with another supervisory authority, intermediate information should be given to the data subject. In order to facilitate the submission of complaints, each supervisory authority should take measures such as providing a complaint submission form which can also be completed electronically, without excluding other means of communication.
rewrite: Every data subject must have the right to file a complaint with one supervisory authority, especially in their Member State of habitual residence, and the right to an effective judicial remedy under Article 47 of the Charter if they believe their rights under this Regulation are violated or if the supervisory authority fails to act on a complaint, partly or fully rejects or dismisses it, or does not take necessary action to protect the data subject’s rights. The investigation after a complaint should be conducted, subject to judicial oversight, as appropriate for the specific case. The supervisory authority must inform the data subject of the complaint’s progress and outcome within a reasonable timeframe. If further investigation or coordination with another supervisory authority is needed, interim updates should be provided to the data subject. To make complaint submission easier, each supervisory authority should implement measures like offering a complaint form that can be filled out electronically, without precluding other communication methods.

text: Where another supervisory authority should act as a lead supervisory authority for the processing activities of the controller or processor but the concrete subject matter of a complaint or the possible infringement concerns only processing activities of the controller or processor in the Member State where the complaint has been lodged or the possible infringement detected and the matter does not substantially affect or is not likely to substantially affect data subjects in other Member States, the supervisory authority receiving a complaint or detecting or being informed otherwise of situations that entail possible infringements of this Regulation should seek an amicable settlement with the controller and, if this proves unsuccessful, exercise its full range of powers. This should include: specific processing carried out in the territory of the Member State of the supervisory authority or with regard to data subjects on the territory of that Member State; processing that is carried out in the context of an offer of goods or services specifically aimed at data subjects in the territory of the Member State of the supervisory authority; or processing that has to be assessed taking into account relevant legal obligations under Member State law.
rewrite: When a different supervisory authority should serve as the lead for a controller’s or processor’s activities, but the specific complaint or potential breach relates only to processing within the Member State where the complaint was filed or the infringement identified, and the issue does not significantly impact or is unlikely to significantly impact data subjects in other Member States, the authority that receives the complaint, detects, or is otherwise informed of possible violations of this Regulation should pursue an amicable resolution with the controller. If this fails, it should then fully employ its powers. This applies to: processing specifically conducted within the supervisory authority’s Member State or concerning data subjects there; processing in connection with an offer of goods or services explicitly targeted at data subjects in that Member State; or processing that must be evaluated considering relevant legal duties under that Member State’s law.

text: In order to ensure that natural persons are not deprived of the protection to which they are entitled under this Regulation, the processing of personal data of data subjects who are in the Union by a controller or a processor not established in the Union should be subject to this Regulation where the processing activities are related to offering goods or services to such data subjects irrespective of whether connected to a payment.
